text: 1/8/2026 Cemetery Management Software 2026 Cemetery Software Buyer’s Guide: Choose the Best System Cemetery managers should consider this when purchasing a cemetery software in 2026. Cemetery management software has become essential for cemeteries, memorial parks, and municipalities seeking to modernize operations, preserve historical records, and improve service to families. In 2026, cemetery software solutions are more powerful than ever but the number of options can make selection challenging. This buyer s guide explains what cemetery software is, which features matter most, and how to choose the right platform , with a look at the most commonly used systems in the market today. Key Features to Look for in Cemetery Software When selecting cemetery software, it's essential to identify key features that will optimize cemetery management. One of the primary features to seek is an intuitive and user-friendly interface. This ensures that all staff members, regardless of their technical expertise, can navigate and utilize the system effectively. A well-designed interface reduces the learning curve and minimizes the risk of errors, which is particularly important in managing sensitive data. Another critical feature is robust data management capabilities. Cemetery software should allow for the efficient handling of records, including burial plots, maintenance schedules, and customer information. The ability to easily store, retrieve, and update records ensures that all information is current and accurate, which is vital for both operational efficiency and regulatory compliance. Additionally, look for software that provides secure data storage and backup options to protect against data loss. Integration with other systems is also a significant feature to consider. Cemetery operations often involve various software applications, such as accounting, customer relationship management (CRM), and geographic information systems (GIS). The ability to integrate seamlessly with these systems can streamline workflows and improve overall efficiency. Look for cemetery software that offers API integration or other interoperability features to ensure smooth communication between different platforms. Benefits of Using Cemetery Management Software Implementing cemetery management software can bring numerous advantages to your operations. One of the most notable benefits is enhanced organizational efficiency. With all data centralized in a single system, staff can quickly access and update information, reducing the time spent on manual record-keeping. This efficiency can lead to faster service delivery and improved customer satisfaction. Another significant advantage is improved accuracy and compliance. Cemetery management involves handling sensitive and legally regulated information. Cemetery software helps ensure that all records are accurate and up-to-date, reducing the risk of errors that could lead to regulatory fines or legal issues. Automated reminders and notifications can help staff stay on top of compliance requirements and maintenance schedules. Additionally, cemetery software can enhance financial management. By integrating with accounting systems, the software can streamline billing and invoicing processes, providing real-time financial insights. This integration helps in tracking revenue, managing expenses, and ensuring that financial records are accurate and transparent. Overall, the financial benefits of cemetery software can lead to better budgeting and resource allocation. Types of Cemetery Software Solutions There are several types of cemetery software solutions available, each catering to different needs and operational scales. On-premise software is one option, where the system is installed locally on the organization s servers. This type of software provides greater control over data and customization but requires significant IT resources for maintenance and updates. It is often preferred by larger cemeteries with the necessary infrastructure and IT support. Cloud-based software is another popular option, offering flexibility and scalability. With cloud-based solutions, data is stored on remote servers and accessed via the internet. This model allows for easy access from any location, making it ideal for cemeteries with multiple sites or remote staff. It also reduces the need for in-house IT maintenance, as updates and backups are managed by the service provider. Hybrid solutions combine elements of both on-premise and cloud-based software. These systems offer the benefits of cloud accessibility while retaining some local control over data. Hybrid solutions can be particularly useful for cemeteries transitioning from traditional systems to modern software, providing a balance between control and convenience. How to Evaluate Cemetery Software Providers When evaluating cemetery software providers, it's important to consider their reputation and experience in the industry. Look for providers with a proven track record of delivering reliable and effective solutions to other cemeteries. Reviews, case studies, and testimonials can provide valuable insights into the provider s reliability and customer satisfaction levels. Make sure to verify the authenticity of these references to ensure they accurately represent the provider's capabilities. Customer support is another crucial factor in the evaluation process. Effective support can make a significant difference in the successful implementation and ongoing use of the software. Assess the provider s support options, including availability, response times, and the range of support services offered. Providers that offer comprehensive training programs, dedicated account managers, and 24/7 support can add significant value to your investment. Finally, consider the provider's commitment to innovation and future development. Cemetery management needs are constantly evolving, and it s important to choose a provider that is dedicated to continuous improvement. Look for providers that actively invest in research and development, regularly update their software, and incorporate user feedback into their development process. This commitment ensures that the software will remain relevant and effective as your needs change. Pricing Models for Cemetery Software Pricing models for cemetery software can vary significantly, and understanding these models is crucial for making an informed decision. One common pricing model is the subscription-based model, where cemeteries pay a recurring fee, typically monthly or annually. This model often includes access to updates, support, and cloud storage, making it a predictable and manageable expense. Subscription-based pricing is particularly advantageous for cemeteries looking to minimize upfront costs and maintain flexibility. Perpetual licensing is another pricing model, where cemeteries pay a one-time fee for the software license. This model provides long-term ownership of the software but may require additional fees for updates, support, and maintenance. Perpetual licensing is often preferred by cemeteries with stable IT budgets and a preference for capital expenditures over operating expenses. Usage-based pricing is a newer model that charges cemeteries based on their actual usage of the software. This model can be cost-effective for smaller cemeteries or those with fluctuating needs, as it aligns costs with usage levels. However, it requires careful monitoring to avoid unexpected expenses. When considering this model, ensure that you understand the usage metrics and any potential overage charges. User Reviews and Testimonials: What to Consider User reviews and testimonials provide valuable insights into the real-world performance and user satisfaction of cemetery software. When considering reviews, it s important to look for patterns in user feedback. Consistent positive feedback on specific features or support services can indicate strengths, while recurring negative comments may highlight potential issues. Pay attention to the context of the reviews to understand how the software performs in similar operational environments to your own. Authenticity and credibility of reviews are also important factors. Verified reviews from reputable sources or industry associations are generally more reliable. Be cautious of overly positive or negative reviews that lack specific details, as they may be biased or fabricated. Seeking out in-depth case studies or reaching out to current users for direct feedback can provide a more comprehensive understanding of the software s strengths and weaknesses. In addition to user reviews, consider the testimonials provided by the software provider. While these are typically positive, they can still offer insights into the provider s customer service, implementation process, and long-term support. Look for testimonials that detail specific benefits and improvements experienced by the user, as these can indicate the potential value of the software for your operations. Implementation and Training for Cemetery Software Successful implementation of cemetery software requires careful planning and execution. Begin by assessing your current processes and identifying areas that will benefit most from automation and digitalization. This assessment will help you outline clear objectives and requirements for the software. Engage with the software provider early in the process to ensure that they understand your needs and can tailor the implementation accordingly. Training is a critical component of successful software adoption. Comprehensive training programs should be provided to all staff members who will use the software. This training should cover basic functionality, advanced features, and best practices for data management. Interactive training sessions, user manuals, and online resources can enhance the learning experience and ensure that staff are confident in using the new system. Ongoing support and training are also important to address any issues that arise post-implementation and to keep staff updated on new features and updates. Regular check-ins with the software provider can help identify and resolve any challenges early on. By investing in thorough training and support, you can ensure a smooth transition and maximize the benefits of your cemetery software. Future Trends in Cemetery Software Technology The landscape of cemetery software technology is continuously evolving, with several emerging trends set to shape the future of cemetery management. One such trend is the increasing use of AI and machine learning. These technologies can enhance data analysis, automate routine tasks, and provide predictive insights for better decision-making. For example, AI can help predict maintenance needs based on historical data, ensuring timely interventions and reducing operational disruptions. Another significant trend is the integration of mobile technologies. As remote work becomes more prevalent, the ability to access and manage cemetery data from mobile devices is becoming increasingly important. Mobile-friendly software solutions enable staff to update records, schedule maintenance, and communicate with families from anywhere, enhancing flexibility and responsiveness. Sustainability is also becoming a focal point in cemetery management. Software solutions that support eco-friendly practices, such as digital record-keeping and paperless transactions, are gaining popularity. Additionally, software that facilitates green burial practices and tracks environmental impact can help cemeteries meet the growing demand for sustainable options. By staying ahead of these trends, cemeteries can ensure they remain relevant and responsive to the needs of their communities. title: FAQ | Cemetery Software - EVERARK
description: Frequently asked questions about cemetery software and EverArk in our cemetery FAQ.
text: FREQUENTY ASKED QUESTIONS PEOPLE OFTEN ASK THESE QUESTIONS ABOUT CEMETERY MANAGEMENT SOFTWARE AND TECHNOLOGY. What is cemetery software? Cemetery software is a specialized digital solution designed to help cemeteries manage their operations, records, and customer interactions more efficiently. It replaces manual processes (like paper maps or spreadsheets) with tools that streamline administration, sales, mapping, and compliance. Why is cemetery software important? Cemetery software is important because it modernizes how cemeteries operate, helping them manage people, property, and paperwork more accurately and efficiently. Without it, cemeteries often rely on outdated, error-prone systems like paper maps, physical file cabinets, or scattered spreadsheets. What are the key features of cemetery management software? Cemetery management software offers digital plot mapping, recordkeeping, sales tracking, customer relationship management, reporting, maintenance scheduling, and compliance tools to streamline cemetery operations. Is cemetery software cloud-based or on-premise? Cemetery software can be either cloud-based or on-premise , but most modern solutions are cloud-based, like EverArk, to offer remote access, automatic updates, and better data security, while some legacy or highly customized systems may still be run on-premise. What are the benefits of cloud-based cemetery software? Cloud-based cemetery software provides secure, remote access to records and maps, automatic updates, real-time collaboration, and reduced IT costs, making cemetery management more efficient and resilient. What is the cost of cemetery management software? The cost of cemetery management software typically ranges from $50 to $500+ per month , depending on factors like the number of users, cemetery size, features included (e.g., mapping, CRM, accounting), and whether it s cloud-based or on-premise; some vendors also charge one-time setup fees or offer custom enterprise pricing for large cemeteries. What security features are included in cemetery software? Cemetery software typically includes security features such as data encryption , user access controls , role-based permissions , audit logs , regular data backups , and secure cloud hosting to protect sensitive records, prevent unauthorized access, and ensure compliance with privacy regulations. Does cemetery software support online payments? Yes, many cemetery software platforms support online payments by integrating with payment gateways (like Stripe, PayPal, or Authorize.net), allowing families to pay for plots, services, or memorials securely through a website or customer portal. EverArk enables integration to Stripe and PayPal How does cemetery software improve cemetery operations? Cemetery software improves operational efficiency by automating tasks like plot assignments, recordkeeping, and work order tracking; centralizing all data in one accessible platform; reducing errors from manual processes; and enabling staff to quickly retrieve information, generate reports, and coordinate services all of which save time and reduce administrative burden. Can cemetery software help with plot mapping? Yes, cemetery software can help with plot mapping by providing interactive digital maps that show the location and status of each plot whether it's available, sold, or occupied allowing staff to easily manage inventory, prevent double sales, and visually guide families during plot selection. Does cemetery software support financial management? Yes, cemetery software often supports financial management by tracking plot sales, managing payment plans, generating invoices and receipts, and producing financial reports sometimes even integrating with accounting systems like QuickBooks or Xero for seamless bookkeeping. How does cemetery software assist in managing cemetery records? Cemetery software assists in managing cemetery records by digitally storing and organizing vital information such as burial permits, deeds, interment history, ownership details, and documents making it easy to search, update, and retrieve records accurately and securely from a centralized database. Can cemetery software integrate with other cloud software? Yes, cemetery software can integrate with other cloud software such as accounting platforms (e.g., QuickBooks), payment gateways , and email or calendar apps , enabling seamless data flow, automation, and enhanced functionality across operations. Typically, a good cemetery software won't integrate with a CRM or mapping system since they'll already have it, like EverArk. What size cemetery should use cemetery software? Cemetery software is beneficial for cemeteries of all sizes from small, rural cemeteries with a few hundred plots to large, municipal or private cemeteries with tens of thousands because it scales to fit the needs of managing records, mapping, and operations efficiently regardless of size. Does cemetery software offer mobile access? Yes, many modern cemetery software solutions offer mobile access through responsive web apps or dedicated mobile apps, allowing staff to view maps, update records, manage tasks, and access information on-site using smartphones or tablets. How does cemetery software enhance customer service? Cemetery software enhances customer service by enabling staff to quickly access plot availability, retrieve records, generate contracts, and communicate with families efficiently often through digital maps, automated reminders, and online portals that provide a more responsive, transparent, and professional experience. Can cemetery software help with historical records management? Yes, cemetery software can help with historical records management by digitizing and preserving old burial records, deeds, and maps making them easily searchable, reducing the risk of loss or damage, and ensuring long-term accessibility for genealogical research, audits, and regulatory compliance. How does automated workflow benefit cemetery operations? Automated workflow benefits cemetery operations by streamlining routine tasks such as plot reservations, service scheduling, document generation, and follow-up reminders reducing manual errors, speeding up processes, improving staff coordination, and freeing up time for more personalized family service and strategic planning. Can families access cemetery records through the software? Yes, many cemetery software platforms offer family portals or public-facing features that allow families to access cemetery records , view plot locations, make reservations, submit information, or pay online enhancing transparency and convenience. How does cemetery software assist in inventory management? Cemetery software assists in inventory management by tracking the status of every plot available, reserved, sold, or occupied on a digital map, maintaining real-time records of inventory levels, and providing tools to manage sales, transfers, and future availability with accuracy and efficiency. Does cemetery software offer reporting and analytics? Yes, cemetery software typically offers reporting and analytics features that generate insights on plot sales, inventory status, interments, financials, maintenance activities, and customer interactions helping cemetery managers make informed decisions and meet regulatory or board reporting requirements. Is training required to use cemetery software? No, not if the cemetery software is easy to use and setup with advanced and user-friendly tutorials and videos, like EverArk. For more outdated solutions, t raining is usually recommended to use cemetery software effectively, especially if the navigation is not intuitive. Can cemetery software assist in scheduling funeral services? Yes, cemetery software can assist in scheduling funeral services by providing tools to book interments, coordinate staff and resources, avoid scheduling conflicts, send reminders, and track service details all from a centralized calendar or workflow system. Does cemetery software offer multilingual support? Yes, many cemetery software platforms offer multilingual support , allowing users and families to access the system in different languages especially helpful for cemeteries serving diverse communities or operating in multilingual regions. How does cemetery software help in managing cemetery staff? Cemetery software helps manage cemetery staff by assigning tasks, tracking work orders, scheduling maintenance, monitoring performance, and enabling internal communication ensuring staff are organized, accountable, and aligned with daily operational needs. What customization options are available in cemetery software? Cemetery software offers customization options such as tailored plot maps, user permissions, branded portals, configurable workflows, custom reports, and integration with accounting or CRM systems. Can cemetery software handle pre-need sales and contracts? Yes, cemetery software can handle pre-need sales and contracts by tracking future plot reservations, managing payment plans, generating legally compliant contracts, and linking them to customer records for seamless long-term planning and service delivery. How do you know if your cemetery needs a cemetery software? You know your cemetery needs cemetery software if you're struggling with disorganized records, outdated maps, inefficient processes, or growing demand for digital services from families and staff. How can cemeteries choose the best software? Cemeteries can choose the best software by evaluating their specific needs such as plot mapping, record management, sales tracking, and online access then comparing features, ease of use, scalability, customer support, integration options, pricing, and user reviews across multiple vendors through demos or trial periods. What trends are shaping cemetery software? Trends shaping cemetery software include cloud and mobile access, GIS-enabled mapping, AI-driven analytics, online memorial features, green burial tracking, and emerging technologies like blockchain and AR/VR for enhanced transparency and customer experience. title: Why Software Implementations Fail | Cemetery Software - EVERARK
description: Getting ready to implement a new cemetery software?  Here's some reasons why implementations fail.
text: 07/11/2023 WHY DO CEMETERY SOFTWARE IMPLEMENTATIONS FAIL? In our last blog, we discussed what is required to successfully implement a cemetery software. This week, we will look at why cemetery software implementations fail. Here are some common factors that contribute to implementation failures: Poor Planning Inadequate planning, including unclear objectives, unrealistic timelines, and insufficient resource allocation, can lead to a cemetery software implementation failure. Lack of a well-defined strategy and project scope can result in misalignment between expectations and outcomes. It is important to understand that implementing a cemetery software is time-consuming, and requires a dedicated team. Inadequate Requirements Gathering Failure to gather and document comprehensive requirements can result in a cemetery software solution that does not meet the needs of the users or the organization. Insufficient involvement of key stakeholders and end-users during the requirements gathering process can lead to misunderstandings and gaps in functionality. Make sure to develop a checklist of requirements that meets the needs of your cemetery and users. Lack of User Involvement Users and stakeholders should be actively involved throughout the cemetery software implementation process. Failure to engage users can result in a solution that does not meet their needs, leading to low adoption rates and resistance to change. Nothing is more important than getting buy-in from the users. Without their willingness to learn and adopt a new system, the implementation is bound to fail. Insufficient Testing and Quality Assurance Neglecting proper testing and quality assurance processes can result in cemetery software that is prone to bugs, errors, and performance issues. Inadequate testing can lead to unexpected problems during implementation or after deployment, negatively impacting the user experience. Once you have lost the confidence of the user base, system adoption can be extremely challenging. Ineffective Project Management Poor project management practices, such as inadequate communication, lack of coordination, scope creep, and insufficient risk management, can derail cemetery software implementations. Without effective project oversight, timelines and budgets can spiral out of control, leading to failure. An experienced project manager that understands the dependencies between scope, budget, timeline, and resources is critical. Incompatibility and Integration Issues Integration challenges arise when new software needs to interact with existing cemetery systems or databases. Incompatible technologies, data migration issues, and inadequate planning for data conversion and system integration can hinder the success of the implementation. Make sure to document a flow chart of your system architecture highlighting data flows. Resistance to Change People's natural resistance to change can impede cemetery software implementation efforts. Lack of user training and change management strategies can lead to a lack of user adoption, dissatisfaction, and ultimately, failure of the software solution. Make sure the cemetery software is intuitive and user-friendly to minimize the resistance of learning a new software. Test and Validate Conduct thorough testing of the cemetery software to identify and resolve any issues or bugs. Develop test scenarios and use cases that cover various functionalities and business processes. Involve end-users in the testing process to gather feedback and ensure the software meets their needs. It is critical for the long-term success of the cemetery software that the end-users are comfortable with the cemetery software before is goes live. Lack of Scalability and Flexibility Cemetery software implementations can fail if they are not designed to accommodate future growth and changing requirements. Inadequate scalability and flexibility can limit the system's ability to adapt to evolving needs, resulting in a short lifespan for the software. Make sure you are working with a software vendor that is open to growth and growing the software in a direction that meets your future growth. Inadequate Budget and Resource Allocation Insufficient funding and resource allocation can restrict the implementation process, leading to compromised quality, delays, and ultimately, failure. An experienced project manager along with dedicated resources, such as stakeholders, can properly manage these risks. It's worth noting that not all cemetery software implementations fail, and many challenges can be mitigated through careful planning, effective project management, and a focus on user engagement and satisfaction. Request a demo of EverArk today to see what we can do to help you mitigate the risks of implementing a new cemetery software. . Previous

text: Last Updated: February 2, 2024 This Privacy Policy describes how Eternal Legacy Company, LLC ( EverArk , we , or us ) collects, uses, and discloses information about you. This Privacy Policy applies to information we collect when you use our digital legacy services and otherwise access or use our websites and mobile apps that link to this Privacy Policy (collectively, our Services ). We may change this Privacy Policy from time to time. If we make material changes, we will notify you by revising the date at the top of this policy. In some cases, we may provide you with additional notice (such as by adding a statement to the Services or sending you a notification). We encourage you to review this Privacy Policy regularly to stay informed about our information practices and the choices available to you. CONTENTS Collection of Information Use of Information Sharing of Information Analytics Your Choices Contact Us COLLECTION OF INFORMATION The information we collect from you varies depending on the way you use our Services. When you browse our public website or use our mobile or web app as a consumer ( Consumer ) to explore our Services, to learn more about us, or to maintain or visit a digital legacy, the information we collect and use is different from the information we collect if you become an EverArk business user ( Business User ) and purchase and/or license one of our products or Services. Below, we describe the different ways we might collect information from you. Information You Provide to Us We collect information you provide directly to us. Consumers For example, when you use our Services as a Consumer, such as when you create your digital legacy using our web app or mobile app we collect your name, email address, phone number, images of you, future resting place, and any other personal information that may be included in a family tree, obituary, funeral notice, eulogy, or other comments on a memorial. Additionally, if you make a donation through the Services, we work with a third-party payment processor to collect and process your payment information. We collect information you provide to us about other people as may be included in a family tree, obituary, funeral notice, eulogy, or comments on a memorial. You are responsible for providing all required notices and obtaining any necessary consent from those other people as needed to provide us with such information. Business Users If you become a Business User, we collect certain personal information from you and/or your authorized users in order to facilitate our business relationship with you and provide you our products and Services (collectively, Business Personal Information ). Business Personal Information we may collect from you and/or your authorized users includes your name, business email address, business phone number, company name, your role at your company, the location of your company, and geolocation data. We also collect information a Business User chooses to provide relating to its customers or individuals that it serves We do not directly collect or control the information our Business Users choose to provide relating to its customers, but rather Business Users determine what information they collect from their business customers, and to the extent EverArk receives that information, we do so on behalf of our Business Users. Information We Collect Automatically When You Use Our Services When you access or use our Services or otherwise transact business with us, we automatically collect certain information, including: Device and Usage Information: We collect information related to your access to and use of the Services, including data about the device and network you use, such as your hardware model, operating system version, mobile network, IP address, unique device identifiers, browser type, how long you spend on a page or screen on the Services, how you interact with our emails, navigation paths between pages or screens, links clicked, and the page you visited before navigating to our Services. Transaction Information : When you make a donation, we collect information about the transaction, such as donation amount, the date and time of the donation, and to whom the donation is directed. Location Information : In accordance with your device permissions, we may collect information about the precise location of your device. You may stop the collection of precise location information at any time (see the Your Choices section below for details). Information Collected by Cookies and Similar Tracking Technologies: We (and our service providers) use tracking technologies, such as cookies, web beacons, and other tracking technologies to collect information about your interactions with the Services, including information about your browsing behavior. Cookies are small data files stored on your hard drive or in device memory that help us improve our Services and your experience, see which areas and features of our Services are popular, and count visits. Web beacons (also known as pixel tags or clear GIFs ) are electronic images that we use on our Services and in our emails to help deliver cookies, count visits, and understand usage and campaign effectiveness. For more information about cookies and how to disable them, see the Your Choices section below. Information We Collect from Other Sources We obtain information from other sources. For example, we may collect information about you from other users of our Services when they add a family tree, obituary, notice, eulogy, or other comments on a memorial. We also collect information from cemeteries regarding plot owners, such as the plot owner s birthday, gender, and date of passing. Additionally, if you create or log into your EverArk account through a third-party platform (such as Google), we will have access to certain information from that platform, such as your name, Google ID, and email address, in accordance with the authorization procedures determined by such platform. USE OF INFORMATION We use the information we collect from or about you in various ways, including to provide, maintain, and improve the Services. We also use the information we collect to: Develop new products and services, including to debug and repair errors in our Services; Personalize your experience with us; Send you technical notices, security alerts, support messages, and other transactional or relationship messages; Communicate with you about products, services, and events offered by EverArk and others, and provide news and information that we think will interest you (see the Your Choices section below for information about how to opt out of these communications at any time); Monitor and analyze trends, usage, and activities in connection with our products and services; Detect, investigate, and help prevent security incidents and other malicious, deceptive, fraudulent, or illegal activity and help protect the rights and property of EverArk and others; Comply with our legal and financial obligations; Create de-identified, anonymized, or aggregated information; and Carry out any other purpose described to you at the time the information was collected. SHARING OF INFORMATION We share personal information in the following circumstances or as otherwise described in this Privacy Policy: We share personal information with vendors that access personal information to perform work for us, such as companies that assist us with web hosting, fraud prevention, customer service, analytics, and marketing and advertising. If you share content on our Services, we share this information publicly with other users of our Services. If you choose to use integrations we offer on our Services, such as sharing your location through our Google maps integration, we may share certain information with the integration partners. We may disclose personal information if we believe that disclosure is in accordance with, or required by, any applicable law or legal process, including lawful requests by public authorities to meet national security or law enforcement requirements. We may share personal information if we believe that your actions are inconsistent with our user agreements or policies, if we believe that you have violated the law, or if we believe it is necessary to protect the rights, property, and safety of EverArk, the public, or others. We may share personal information in connection with, or during negotiations concerning, any merger, sale of company assets, financing, or acquisition of all or a portion of our business by another company. Personal information may be shared between and among EverArk and our future parents, affiliates, and subsidiaries and other companies under common control and ownership. ANALYTICS We engage others to provide analytics services across the web and in mobile apps. These entities may use cookies, web beacons, device identifiers, and other technologies to collect information about your use of our Services and other websites and applications, including your IP address, web browser, mobile network information, pages viewed, time spent on pages or in mobile apps, links clicked, and conversion information. Please note that removing or rejecting cookies could affect the availability and functionality of our Services. For more information about interest-based ads, or to opt out of having your web browsing information collected via tracking technologies and used for behavioral advertising purposes, please visit www.aboutads.info/choices. text: 4/15/2026 Cemetery Management Software Exploring Tech in Cemeteries: Drones, GPS & Mapping Tools Discover how cutting-edge technology like drones, GPS, and mapping tools is reshaping cemeteries, enhancing memorial experiences, and preserving history. The Role of Drones in Cemetery Management Drones are revolutionizing various industries, and cemetery management is no exception. These aerial devices offer a bird's-eye view of vast cemetery landscapes, which is particularly useful for large or historic sites where traditional mapping and surveying methods fall short. By deploying drones, cemetery managers can capture high-resolution images and create detailed maps, ensuring accurate documentation of grave plots and other significant landmarks. This aerial perspective not only facilitates better space management but also helps in identifying areas that require maintenance or development. In addition to mapping and surveying, drones can play a crucial role in enhancing security within cemeteries. These sites are often targets for vandalism and theft, and traditional security measures may not cover every nook and cranny. Drones equipped with surveillance cameras can patrol the grounds, offering real-time footage and immediate alerts in case of suspicious activities. This added layer of security helps preserve the sanctity of these hallowed grounds, ensuring that they remain a respectful place for mourning and remembrance. Furthermore, drones can be instrumental in documenting and preserving the historical and cultural significance of cemeteries. Many cemeteries are home to intricate monuments, statues, and gravestones that have historical and artistic value. Drones can capture detailed images and videos of these artifacts, creating a digital archive that can be used for educational purposes, virtual tours, or restoration projects. By leveraging drone technology, cemetery managers can ensure that the rich heritage of these sites is preserved for future generations. GPS Technology: Enhancing Navigation and Mapping GPS technology has become an integral part of our daily lives, guiding us to our destinations with pinpoint accuracy. In the context of cemeteries, GPS offers a powerful tool for navigation and mapping, making it easier for visitors to locate specific gravesites and memorials. Traditional methods of finding a grave often involve cumbersome maps and relying on staff for assistance. With GPS-enabled devices and applications, visitors can simply input the name or plot number, and the technology will guide them to the exact location, saving time and reducing frustration. Beyond assisting visitors, GPS technology plays a significant role in cemetery management and operations. Accurate mapping of the cemetery grounds is essential for efficient space utilization and future planning. GPS devices can be used to survey the land, marking the precise location of each grave plot and other key features. This data can then be integrated into digital maps and databases, providing a comprehensive overview of the site. Such detailed mapping ensures that no space is wasted and helps in planning future expansions or landscaping projects. Moreover, GPS technology can assist in maintaining accurate records and ensuring compliance with legal and regulatory requirements. Cemeteries often have to adhere to specific guidelines regarding the placement and spacing of graves. By using GPS for precise measurements, cemetery managers can ensure that they are in compliance with these regulations. Additionally, GPS data can be invaluable in case of disputes or legal issues, providing concrete evidence of the exact location and boundaries of grave plots. Innovative Mapping Tools for Cemetery Layouts Innovative mapping tools are transforming the way cemeteries are designed and managed. Traditional paper maps and grids are being replaced by sophisticated software that offers dynamic and interactive mapping solutions. These digital tools allow cemetery managers to create detailed, scalable maps that can be easily updated and shared. With features like layering, zooming, and real-time updates, these maps provide a comprehensive and user-friendly way to manage cemetery layouts. One of the key advantages of using digital mapping tools is the ability to integrate various types of data. For example, Geographic Information Systems (GIS) can combine spatial data with other information such as burial records, maintenance schedules, and historical data. This integrated approach provides a holistic view of the cemetery, making it easier to manage and plan. Cemetery managers can quickly identify available plots, monitor the condition of existing graves, and plan for future developments. The ability to visualize this data on a digital map enhances decision-making and operational efficiency. In addition to improving internal management, digital mapping tools can significantly enhance the visitor experience. Many cemeteries are now offering interactive maps on their websites or through mobile applications. These tools allow visitors to search for specific gravesites, view detailed information about the deceased, and even take virtual tours of the cemetery. By providing easy access to this information, cemeteries can offer a more personalized and engaging experience for visitors, helping them connect with their loved ones and the history of the site. Benefits of Using Technology in Cemetery Operations The adoption of technology in cemetery operations offers numerous benefits that extend beyond simple convenience. One of the most significant advantages is improved accuracy and efficiency in record-keeping. Traditional methods of maintaining burial records can be prone to errors and inconsistencies. Digital databases, on the other hand, ensure that all information is accurately recorded and easily retrievable. This reduces the risk of mistakes and ensures that cemetery managers have access to up-to-date information when making decisions. Another major benefit is enhanced space management. Cemeteries are finite spaces, and efficient use of available land is crucial for long-term sustainability. Technologies such as GPS and digital mapping tools enable precise plotting of gravesites, ensuring that no space is wasted. This level of precision also facilitates better planning for future expansions and helps in identifying areas that can be repurposed or developed. As a result, cemeteries can maximize their capacity and continue to serve their communities for generations to come. Technology also plays a vital role in improving communication and transparency with families and the public. Many cemeteries now offer online portals where families can access burial records, purchase plots, and even schedule maintenance services. This level of transparency builds trust and ensures that families feel involved and informed. Additionally, technologies such as drones and surveillance cameras enhance security, providing peace of mind to families that their loved ones' resting places are being protected. Case Studies: Successful Implementation of Tech in Cemeteries Several cemeteries around the world have successfully implemented technology to enhance their operations and visitor experience. One notable example is Arlington National Cemetery in the United States. Known for its historical significance and vast expanse, Arlington has integrated GPS and digital mapping tools to manage its over 400,000 graves. Visitors can use a dedicated mobile app to locate specific gravesites, view information about the deceased, and even take guided tours of the cemetery. This technology has made it easier for families to connect with their loved ones and explore the rich history of the site. Another example is the Highgate Cemetery in London, a historic site known for its Victorian architecture and famous residents. Highgate has employed drones to capture high-resolution images of the cemetery, creating detailed maps that are used for both management and preservation purposes. The aerial footage has also been used to create virtual tours, allowing people from around the world to explore this iconic cemetery from the comfort of their homes. This innovative use of technology has not only improved operational efficiency but also broadened the reach and accessibility of the site. In Australia, the Rookwood Cemetery has embraced a range of technologies to enhance its operations. Rookwood uses GIS software to create detailed maps of its vast grounds, integrating burial records and maintenance schedules into a single, comprehensive system. The cemetery also offers an online portal where families can search for gravesites, view records, and even leave virtual flowers and messages. This combination of technologies has streamlined operations and provided a more engaging and personalized experience for visitors. Challenges and Considerations in Adopting Technology While the benefits of adopting technology in cemeteries are clear, there are also several challenges and considerations that must be addressed. One of the primary challenges is the cost of implementing and maintaining advanced technologies. Drones, GPS devices, and sophisticated mapping software require significant financial investment, which may be prohibitive for smaller or less-funded cemeteries. Additionally, ongoing maintenance and updates can add to the overall cost, making it essential for cemetery managers to carefully evaluate the return on investment. Another consideration is the need for training and expertise. The successful implementation of technology requires skilled personnel who are proficient in operating and maintaining these tools. This may involve hiring new staff or providing training for existing employees, both of which can be time-consuming and costly. Furthermore, as technology continues to evolve, ongoing education and training will be necessary to keep pace with new developments and ensure that the cemetery is utilizing the latest and most effective tools. Privacy and data security are also critical considerations when adopting technology in cemeteries. Digital databases and online portals often contain sensitive information about the deceased and their families. It is essential to implement robust security measures to protect this data from unauthorized access and breaches. Additionally, the use of drones and surveillance cameras must be carefully managed to respect the privacy of visitors and comply with legal regulations. Cemetery managers must strike a balance between leveraging technology for operational efficiency and maintaining the dignity and privacy of the site. Future Trends: What’s Next for Cemetery Technology? As technology continues to advance, several emerging trends are poised to further transform cemetery management and operations. One such trend is the use of augmented reality (AR) to enhance the visitor experience. AR can overlay digital information onto the physical world, allowing visitors to view interactive displays, historical information, and even virtual reconstructions of monuments and gravesites. This technology can provide a richer and more immersive experience, helping visitors connect with the history and significance of the cemetery. Another promising trend is the use of blockchain technology for secure and transparent record-keeping. Blockchain offers a decentralized and tamper-proof way to store and manage data, ensuring that burial records and other sensitive information are secure and immutable. By adopting blockchain, cemeteries can enhance the integrity and security of their records. text: 4/19/2022 Current Technology Trends in the Death Care Industry The well-known adage says the only sure things in life are death and taxes. The industries that deal with death are embracing technology which not only helps cemeteries and funeral homes become more streamlined, but also lets people s legacies live on after they pass. Cemeteries and Funeral Homes Have Entered Cyberspace People no longer need to go to cemeteries and funeral homes to purchase burial plots, urns, tombstones, or other funerary products and services. When a loved one dies, immediate family members can go online to find everything they need. EverArk is a unique cemetery management and digital legacy software that revolutionizing the death industry. In addition to making the funerary process more streamlined for surviving family and friends, it allows individuals to create a digital legacy in preparation of their own death. After all, everyone should be remembered in the way they see fit. EverArk s innovative software and digital legacy tool gives everyone the power to tell their life story and feature meaningful photos and videos that can be cherished for generations. Interactive Headstones Have a Tale to Tell QR codes are not just for product information and advertising anymore. Today, they can be found on gravestones! When a person visits the burial site of a loved one that has an interactive headstone, they can use their smartphone to scan the QR code that is engraved on the tombstone. Within seconds, they can read all about the person and enjoy seeing them come to life through photos and videos. Digital headstones also come in the form of weatherproof touchscreens that are positioned over a person s final resting place. Through this technology, visitors can learn all about the decedent s life through videos, images, and text without the use of a smartphone. After the first digital tombstone was erected in Slovenia, this technology has become more popular. Crowdfunded Funerals are Easing the Burden It is no secret that funerals are expensive, and rising inflation is making matters worse. When a person dies, it is often unexpected. Immediate family members are left wondering how they can afford to give their loved one the memorial service they deserve. Crowdfunding has helped people pay for everything from startup businesses to lifesaving pet surgeries, and now people can contribute funds that will help pay for some or all the costs associated with a funeral. Webcasting is Helping Everyone Pay Their Respects Traveling to attend a funeral or memorial can often be difficult. Not only is travel expensive, but COVID restrictions present unique challenges. Some airlines still offer bereavement fare, but this special ticketing is not available to friends of the deceased. With the help of high-speed internet technology, webcasting funeral and memorial services is bringing everyone together. title: Death Care Services Trends | Cemetery Software - EVERARK
description: Navigating the future of death care services can be challenging.  Here's some trends, innovations and what you need to know.
text: 04/1/2025 NAVIGATING THE FUTURE OF DEATH CARE SERVICES: Trends, Innovations, and What You Need to Know As the world evolves, so too do the ways we approach death and the services that accompany it. The future of death care services is being shaped by emerging trends and innovative solutions that address the changing needs and expectations of society. From eco-friendly burial options to digital memorialization, modern families are seeking more personalized and meaningful experiences during their time of grief. This article delves into the latest developments in the death care industry, exploring how technology, environmental consciousness, and cultural shifts are redefining traditional practices. Whether you're a professional in the field or someone interested in understanding these changes, navigating the future of death care services is essential. Join us as we uncover what's ahead and arm yourself with the knowledge you need to make informed decisions in this evolving landscape of care and remembrance. Current Trends in Death Care Services The death care industry has witnessed significant shifts over the past few decades, driven by changing societal attitudes and advances in technology. One of the most notable current trends is the increasing preference for cremation over traditional burial. Factors such as cost-effectiveness, environmental concerns, and the desire for more flexible memorialization options have contributed to this shift. Cremation rates have been steadily rising, and it is expected that they will continue to do so, with more families opting for this method of disposition. Another emerging trend is the growing demand for personalized funeral services. Modern consumers are moving away from the one-size-fits-all approach and are instead seeking unique ways to honor their loved ones. This has led to the rise of customized memorial services that reflect the individual s personality, interests, and life story. From themed funerals to incorporating multimedia elements, personalization is becoming a key aspect of death care services. Additionally, there is a noticeable shift towards celebrating life rather than mourning death. This change in perspective is leading to the popularity of life celebrations and memorials that focus on the positive aspects of the deceased's life. These gatherings often include storytelling, music, and other elements that create a more uplifting atmosphere. This trend is reshaping how people perceive and experience funerals, making them more of a tribute to the person's life rather than a somber farewell. Innovations Shaping the Future of Death Care The death care industry is not immune to the wave of innovation sweeping through various sectors. One of the most groundbreaking innovations is the development of biodegradable urns and caskets. These products are designed to break down naturally over time, reducing the environmental impact of traditional burial practices. Companies are also exploring new materials, such as mushroom mycelium and organic fibers, to create sustainable and eco-friendly burial options. Another significant innovation is the advent of space burials. Companies like Celestis offer services that send a portion of the deceased's ashes into space, providing a unique and awe-inspiring way to commemorate their life. This option appeals to those with a passion for space exploration or a desire for an extraordinary final resting place. While space burials are still relatively niche, they represent a growing interest in unconventional memorialization methods. The use of virtual reality (VR) in death care is also gaining traction. VR technology allows families to create immersive memorial experiences, enabling them to revisit cherished memories and moments with their loved ones. This innovation is particularly beneficial for individuals who may not be able to attend physical memorial services due to distance or other constraints. VR memorials offer a new dimension of connection and remembrance, making it possible to honor the deceased in a highly personalized and engaging manner. The Rise of Green and Eco-Friendly Burial Options Environmental consciousness is increasingly influencing various aspects of our lives, and death care services are no exception. The rise of green and eco-friendly burial options reflects a growing awareness of the environmental impact of traditional burial practices. One such option is natural or green burial, which involves interring the body in a biodegradable casket or shroud without the use of embalming fluids. This method allows the body to decompose naturally, returning nutrients to the earth and minimizing the ecological footprint. Aquamation, also known as alkaline hydrolysis, is another eco-friendly alternative to traditional cremation. This process uses water, heat, and alkaline chemicals to break down the body, resulting in a liquid solution and bone fragments. Aquamation has a significantly lower carbon footprint compared to flame-based cremation and does not release harmful emissions into the atmosphere. As awareness of its environmental benefits grows, aquamation is becoming an increasingly popular choice for those seeking sustainable end-of-life options. The concept of conservation burial is also gaining momentum. This approach involves burying the deceased in protected natural areas, such as forests or meadows, where the land is preserved for conservation purposes. Conservation burials not only provide a serene and natural resting place but also contribute to the protection and restoration of natural habitats. This eco-friendly option resonates with individuals who wish to leave a positive environmental legacy and support the preservation of natural landscapes. Technology's Impact on Death Care Services Technology is revolutionizing the death care industry in numerous ways, enhancing both the services provided and the overall experience for families. One significant technological advancement is the use of online memorial platforms. These platforms allow friends and family members to create digital tributes, share memories, and express condolences. Online memorials provide a space for ongoing connection and remembrance, making it easier for people to honor their loved ones regardless of geographical distance. Another area where technology is making a significant impact is in the management of funeral homes and cemeteries. Software solutions are streamlining various administrative tasks, from scheduling services to tracking inventory. These tools improve efficiency and accuracy, allowing funeral directors to focus more on providing compassionate care to grieving families. Additionally, technology is enabling better communication between funeral homes and clients, with features such as online booking and live streaming of services. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning in death care services is also emerging as a transformative trend. AI-powered chatbots can assist families in planning funerals, answering questions, and providing information on various services. Machine learning algorithms can analyze data to identify trends and preferences, helping funeral homes tailor their offerings to meet the needs of their clients. These technological advancements are enhancing the overall experience for families and ensuring that services are more personalized and efficient. Understanding Consumer Preferences in Death Care Understanding consumer preferences is crucial for the death care industry, as it allows providers to offer services that align with the evolving needs and expectations of families. One notable shift in consumer preferences is the increasing demand for transparency and information. Modern consumers are more informed and discerning, seeking detailed information about the services and products they are considering. This has led to a greater emphasis on clear communication, with funeral homes and death care providers offering comprehensive explanations of their offerings and pricing. Another significant trend is the preference for pre-planning funeral arrangements. More individuals are choosing to make their end-of-life plans in advance, ensuring that their wishes are respected and relieving their families of the burden of making decisions during a difficult time. Pre-planning allows for greater personalization and can also be a financial consideration, as individuals can lock in current prices and avoid future cost increases. This proactive approach is becoming more common as people recognize the benefits of having their affairs in order. Cultural and generational differences also play a role in shaping consumer preferences in death care services. For example, younger generations may be more open to alternative and innovative burial options, while older generations may prefer traditional practices. Additionally, cultural and religious beliefs can influence preferences for certain types of services and rituals. Understanding these nuances is essential for death care providers to offer meaningful and respectful services that honor the diverse needs of their clients. The Role of Personalization in Death Care Services Personalization is becoming a cornerstone of modern death care services, as families seek to create meaningful and unique tributes to their loved ones. One way personalization is being achieved is through the incorporation of personal artifacts and mementos into memorial services. Items such as photographs, letters, and cherished belongings can be displayed or included in the ceremony, providing a tangible connection to the deceased and celebrating their individuality. Another aspect of personalization is the customization of the service itself. This can include selecting specific readings, music, and themes that reflect the life and personality of the deceased. Some families may choose to have a themed funeral that aligns with the interests or passions of their loved one, such as a sports-themed service for an avid fan or a nature-inspired ceremony for an outdoor enthusiast. These personalized touches create a more intimate and meaningful experience for those in attendance. The use of technology is also enhancing personalization in death care services. For example, digital slideshows and video tributes can be created to showcase the life and memories of the deceased. These multimedia elements can be played during the service or shared online, allowing family and friends to participate in the memorial from anywhere in the world. Additionally, personalized memorial websites and social media pages provide a platform for ongoing remembrance and connection, enabling loved ones to share stories, photos, and messages long after the service has concluded. Regulatory Changes Affecting the Death Care Industry The death care industry is subject to various regulations and standards that ensure the dignity and safety of end-of-life services. One significant regulatory change that has impacted the industry is the increased scrutiny of cremation practices. As cremation rates have risen, regulators have introduced stricter guidelines to ensure that cremation facilities operate safely and ethically. These regulations address aspects such as emissions control, proper handling of remains, and transparent reporting, ensuring that cremation services meet high standards of care. Another area of regulatory focus is the licensing and training of death care professionals. Governments and industry organizations are placing greater emphasis on the education and certification of funeral directors, embalmers, and other practitioners. This ensures that professionals have the necessary skills and knowledge to provide compassionate and competent care. Continuing education requirements are also being implemented to keep practitioners informed about the latest developments and best practices in the field. title: Digitizing Cemetery Records | Cemetery Software - EVERARK
description: How do you digitize your cemetery records?  Here's a step-by-step process to get rid of paper documents and transition to all digital records.
text: 11/02/2023 HOW DO YOU DIGITIZE YOUR CEMETERY RECORDS? In an earlier blog, we discussed why your cemetery should consider transitioning from paper records to digital records . Digitizing cemetery records is a valuable step for efficiency and accessibility. Here's a general step-by-step process to help you with the transition: Assessment: Evaluate the current record system and identify what needs to be digitized. This may include burial plots, interment records, maps, and more. It's not uncommon to have interment cards and sales contracts in abundance. Knowing how many records you need to digitize is the first step towards assembling a transition plan. Choose Software: Select cemetery management software or create a custom database. Ensure it meets your specific needs for record-keeping and retrieval. Your records need to be well organized and easily accessible. These should be the two most important aspects when deciding what cemetery system to implement and use. Data Entry: Enter existing records into the digital system. This can be a time-consuming process but is crucial for accuracy. Using a company that specializes in digitizing records is a great way to simplify this task as it can be very overwhelming. Scanning individual records and making sure they are saved such that they can be easily imported into a system is critical. Digital Maps: Create digital maps of the cemetery to help locate burial plots. GIS (Geographic Information System) software can be helpful for this. Paper maps are cumbersome so moving to a system that has interactive, digital maps will help your sales team and customers view plots. Backup and Security: Implement data backup and security measures to protect against data loss and unauthorized access. Again, selecting and implementing the right cemetery software will mitigate your risk of data loss. Cloud-based software hosted on major providers such as Google or AWS will back up your cemetery data. Accessibility: Make the records accessible through a user-friendly interface, possibly a website or a kiosk at the cemetery. Implementing a software where your records can be retrieved and reviewed quickly is very important. If the cemetery software takes more than 3 clicks to locate and view records, consider another system. Training: Train staff on how to use the digital system effectively. The ease-of-use of a cemetery software is extremely important for staff to adopt the new system. However, making sure they're trained so they know how to access the correct information efficiently is critical for long-term success. Maintenance: Regularly update and maintain the digital records to reflect new interments, changes, and corrections. It's not enough just to upload old records and save them. It's also important to make sure older records are updated with current information and policies. Archiving: Keep physical copies of records as a backup and for historical purposes. Just because you're going digital doesn't mean you have to discard all your old paper copies. It never hurts to archive your paper records so you can go back to them if you need. title: Fun Funeral Facts | Cemetery Software - EVERARK
description: Funeral details are often rooted in tradition and beliefs. Learn some interesting facts about funerals that might surprise you.
text: 8/3/2022 facts about funerals that might surprise you When most people think about funerals, they imagine a somber ceremony with flowers, prayers, and people dressed in black conversing quietly amongst themselves. While this is true in most cases, modern funerals do not always follow this format. Funeral details are often rooted in tradition and beliefs. Nevertheless, heartfelt funerary rituals vary, which is why each one is beautifully unique. The Reasons Behind Today s Funeral Practices If you have ever wondered why we place flowers on graves or if funerals can be boisterous occasions, read on! Romans Inspired the Use of Gravestones When Rome controlled Britain, Roman soldiers erected gravestones close to military forts and Romano-British settlements. This was done to mark the passing of women and children. Roman soldiers were not allowed to marry, so placing gravestones where they could be viewed often was their way of showing respect for the people they cared about. This practice also legitimized the relationship they were unable to have while the woman or child was alive. During the fifth century, Rome lost control of Britain and the ritual of erecting gravestones ended until the modern era resurrected the tradition. Burials Were a Family Affair Literally Throughout the Anglo-Saxon period, people who chose cremation were not buried immediately. The urn holding their ashes remained in the community until several members of the decedent s family had died, then all the urns were buried together within a large mound of earth called a barrow. Mourning for Money Moirologists are professional mourners who are hired to attend a funeral. While this may seem odd, it is an ancient tradition that spans the globe and is even mentioned in the Old and New Testaments. It is believed that the practice of hiring moirologists started in China and the Middle East, but this is difficult to pinpoint. There is also evidence of moirologists were employed throughout Egypt. Prior to the 20th century, European families would hire professional mourners to look sad and wail. In Rome, there are accounts of professional mourners attending the funerals of wealthy individuals. Their presence signified that the decedent was part of high society. The moirologists would cry loudly during the burial as they pulled on their hair and clothing. They would even scratch at their face to make their act more dramatic. Today, moirologists are still making a living; however, they are usually hired when the deceased has few living relatives, so their main job is to increase attendance. In South Africa, hired mourners behave similarly to how they acted 2,000 years ago and will even threaten to jump into the grave, but this level of drama comes with an additional fee. Adorning Graves with Flowers Placing flowers on graves is an old tradition. It is believed they bring goodwill to the deceased, and each type of flower carries its own meaning. Roses are placed on a grave to symbolize love, hope, and beauty. Two roses joined together represent a strong bond and are usually placed on a couple s gravesite. Meanwhile, rose buds are laid on the graves of children, and a rose that is partially open is set on the grave of teenagers to symbolize a life cut short. A rose in full bloom symbolizes that the grave belongs to someone who died in the prime of life. Lilies are another popular gravesite flower as they represent innocence and purity. The Easter lily symbolizes resurrection and innocence of the soul. Lily of the Valley signifies innocence, humility, and renewal. If you pass by an older cemetery in the springtime, you are sure to see daffodils springing from the graves. People planted these flower bulbs because they symbolize grace, beauty, and deep regard. Daisies are another common cemetery flower as they represent gentleness and innocence. If you happen to find a grave covered in ivy, the person who planted it wanted to convey faithfulness, undying affection, and eternal life. Waking the Dead Irish wakes are anything but solemn. While wakes are more informal than funerals, Irish tradition involved playing loud music in the hopes it would ward off evil spirits. However, blasting tunes also served the purpose of ensuring that the person was indeed dead. Ushering the Departed Oftentimes, when a hearse arrives at the cemetery, the funeral director will walk in front of the hearse to guide the driver toward the gravesite. This long-standing tradition dates back to the days when horse drawn carriages delivered bodies to cemeteries. Regardless of when the practice started, guiding the hearse will always be a funeral director s way of showing respect for the decedent. The Original Green Burial During medieval times, the family of the deceased borrowed or leased a community coffin to transport the body of their loved one from the home to the churchyard. This was performed by the parish church. After arriving at the gravesite, the deceased was removed from the coffin and wrapped in a shroud before being placed into the grave. Saying Hello to a New Tradition of Bidding Good-bye The timeless traditions of placing flowers on graves and playing music during the service will always be a way for the living to find comfort while honoring the dead. However, flowers wither and every song has a final note. With the advent of technology, people can create a digital legacy that will last forever. A digital legacy is a collection of photos and videos of a deceased person that is uploaded to the internet. These virtual albums often include the person s favorite music. Usually, the decedent s loved ones will create the digital legacy to share with others, but it is sometimes featured at the funeral or wake as well. People are even fashioning their own digital legacy prior to their death, so they can be remembered in their own special way. EverArk is the premier software that is making digital legacies the newest funerary tradition. Its user-friendly format allows loved ones to easily upload, view, and share cherished memories of deceased family members and friends. EverArk is even being used by people to create their own digital legacy prior to their death. They appreciate the peace of mind this state-of-the-art software provides as it assures them that their legacy will live on to show future generations what they were like when they were alive. While older traditions will always remain, it is easy to see how digital legacies are blazing the trail for a new tradition. After all, everyone should be remembered in their best light and the internet is a surefire pathway to keeping a loved one s spirit shining brightly. If you are interested in being a trailblazer by creating a digital legacy for yourself or a loved one who has passed on, request a demo of EverArk today! Previous Next

title: Fun Facts About Morticians | Cemetery Software - EVERARK
description: Have you ever considered a career as a mortician, AKA undertaker, funeral director, or embalmer? Read some fun and interesting facts about morticians.
text: 4/28/2022 Fun Facts About Being a Mortician Being a mortician is not always at the top of high school or college graduates career wish lists, but it is an interesting and necessary profession. Those that do choose this occupation consider it to be a higher calling. The term mortician was invented by the funeral industry to replace the word undertaker. They are also known as funeral directors or embalmers and must have an associate or a bachelor s degree in mortuary science. Morticians must be knowledgeable in the preservation process and have a solid understanding of biology as well as a general grasp of business practices. While a mortician s main responsibility is preparing the bodies of the deceased, they also take the stress off grieving families by setting up funerals, communicating with cemeteries and hospitals, and handling important paperwork. Little known facts about morticians: They don t drive hearses to pick up decedents. These days most morticians use minivans or white cargo vans to pick up bodies. Hearses are usually only used for transporting the prepared body to funerals and cemeteries. Believe it or not, hearses are not allowed to travel in HOV lanes because the body is considered cargo. It runs in the family. Many people become funeral directors because they were born into the business and helped with odd jobs during their childhood. The most successful family funeral homes collaborate and blend tradition with fresh ideas. They must repair donor and autopsied bodies. Morticians have reported that this is often an extremely difficult task. Given the circumstances, they appreciate it when family members choose cremation if it does not violate their religious beliefs. They must wash and disinfect the body. A mortician gives a person their very last bath. They are also responsible for washing the hair and styling it. They are makeup artists. Morticians know how to make the dead look more like they did in life. Applying makeup on a body is different than putting it on living skin. I have used regular cosmetics for embalmed bodies, but the skin is so firm, there s no way to work in your foundation. Using an airbrush gets you streak-free, nice coverage. Jaime Reed, Embalmer They rise to the challenge. Morticians do their best to honor the wishes of the deceased and their loved ones. Requests can sometimes seem outlandish, but funeral directors do their best to accommodate. "My grandfather was a mortician. He told me that he had a request one time for dirt to be put in the dead guy's socks. Not just any dirt though dirt from the road the guy lived on since he grew up. My grandfather honored their wish, and the family was very pleased." - Buzzfeed Alternative Morticians Are Becoming Mainstream While death itself will never change, how it is handled is evolving. Alternative morticians are advocates of home funerals and eco-friendly burials, which are also called green burials. For a burial to be eco-friendly, the body must be preserved in a manner that will not harm the environment. This means that the deceased cannot be embalmed with formaldehyde, which is a toxin. Safe substitutes involve refrigeration or dry ice, but there are chemicals morticians can use such as ENIGMA ecobalming fluids that provide temporary preservation. Alternative morticians are very familiar with their community s digital cemeteries. Not only do these modern graveyards offer green burial services, but they rely on EverArk digital cemetery management software to strengthen their communication with morticians. As a result, the decedent s loved ones can grieve with the peace of mind that all their wishes will be carried out properly and with the utmost respect. A mortician s job is never easy. However, when the inevitable happens, they do all they can to make the experience peaceful and pleasantly memorable for all involved.
