title: A Peaceful Rest Beneath the Waves | Cemetery Software - EVERARK
description: Green burials are quickly becoming a popular choice over traditional burials for the environmentally conscious.
text: 11/16/2022 GREEN BURIAL: A PEACEFUL REST BENEATH THE WAVES Green burials are quickly becoming a popular choice over traditional burials for the environmentally conscious. Green burials do not involve formaldehyde-based embalming fluids, concrete burials vaults, or metal caskets because they consume precious resources such as land and wreak havoc on our delicate ecosystem. Blue is the New Green Some people who want to give back to the Earth for their final farewell are opting to be buried at sea. Being buried at sea is one of the greenest ways to have your body become one with nature upon your death. There are several environmentally friendly options available to those who wish to have a peaceful rest in a watery grave. Become Part of an Ocean Habitat One of the most promising ocean burials is available from Memorial Reefs International . This innovative company has partnered with the Reef Ball Foundation to support the survival of fish and other marine organisms by turning cremated remains into artificial reefs. Memorial Reefs International is dedicated to helping people and the environment by providing unique green burials. By combining cremations with a pH balanced concrete mix, a textured hollow sphere called a reef ball is created. Next, a bronze plaque with details about the decedent is affixed to its front. The reef ball is then lowered to the ocean floor where its rough surface and empty interior instantly attract fish, coral polyps, and other aquatic wildlife. Before long, the Memorial Reef becomes an integral part of a thriving marine habitat. After the ceremony, the decedent s loved ones receive the Reef Memorial s GPS coordinates, so they can visit anytime they like. Divers are even allowed to explore the Memorial Reefs but are cautioned against touching the Reef Memorials and doing anything that disturbs marine life. Marine Reefs International offers three reef ball sizes and provides a choice of funeral services. The company can even combine the ashes of two individuals in the event a person wants to be interred with the cremains of their spouse or beloved pet. Marine Reefs International is proud to provide its unique green burial services in Mexico at their Silver Memorial Reef, in Italy at their Venice Memorial Reef, and in New Jersey at their New Jersey Memorial Reef. The company also has established reef ball sites off the coast of Florida, Texas, British Columbia, and Ontario, and announced on February 28 th of this year that they will be placing Memorial Reefs in Hawaii. Float Among the Waves A company called Ocean Ashes is eliminating the need for expensive traditional burials and sprawling cemeteries by giving people the option of releasing their ashes into the deep blue sea. This type of green burial utilizes the ocean currents to force the spread of a person s cremations, so they travel throughout the tranquil cerulean water flowing all over the world. Being interred in this manner is especially eco friendly and life sustaining because the dearly departed becomes part of the amazing aquatic life cycle of countless plant and animal species. Ocean Ashes operates in Florida and offers scattering cruises on private charters that depart from Destin, Saint Petersburg, Islamorada, and the Florida Keys. Green Burial in the Deep Blue When we hear about people being buried at sea, the decedents are usually sailors. The fact is, anyone can be cast into the ocean upon their death if this is how they choose to be interred. Thirty days before the burial, a general permit from the EPA must be filled out and submitted per federal regulations in accordance with the Marine Protection, Research and Sanctuaries Act. The permit authorizes the transportation and burial of both cremated and non-cremated human remains into the ocean. However, specific conditions must be met. First, the unembalmed remains cannot be released into the sea within three nautical miles of shore, and second, the attendees cannot toss anything into the water that is not decomposable such as plastic or metal flowers, wreaths, and gravestones or monuments. If loved ones want to have such items accompany the burial, they must submit a special permit . While the body can be inside a casket when it is placed into the ocean, a truly green sea burial involves the decedent being wrapped in a natural fiber shroud. A steel chain is then secured around the body to help it sink to the seafloor quickly and remain submerged. It is important to note that medical waste such as pacemakers, artificial joints, pins, and other surgical implants must be removed from the body or cremations prior to the ocean burial. The Sea Offers the Greenest Burials People who want an earth friendly burial are smart to choose a saltwater grave. These types of burials are the most ecological because no toxic chemicals are involved, and the body decomposes quickly as it becomes part of the ocean s lifecycle. For your final farewell, it does not matter if you want to become part of an artificial reef or be ceremoniously cast into the vast blue sea, you will be helping the earth by making as little impact as possible upon your death. Just be sure to make your wishes known or you may end up embalmed and laid to rest in a traditional cemetery. title: How to Map a Cemetery | Cemetery Software - EVERARK
description: What is the easiest way to map your cemetery and what steps should you consider?
text: 2/12/2024 WHAT IS THE EASIEST WAY TO MAP YOUR CEMETERY? Mapping a cemetery can vary in complexity depending on the size and layout of the cemetery and the level of detail you want to include. Here are some steps you can follow to map a cemetery: 1. Plan and Prepare: Before you start mapping, it's helpful to plan your approach. Determine the boundaries of the cemetery and decide how detailed you want your map to be. Make sure you have permission to map the cemetery, as some may have restrictions on photography or mapping activities. 2. Gather Tools: You'll need some basic tools for mapping, such as a measuring tape, a compass, and possibly a GPS device or smartphone with mapping apps. Capturing GPS coordinates is especially important for cemetery management software and online, interactive mapping. You may also want to bring a camera or sketchpad to document details of the cemetery. 3. Walk the Cemetery: Walk through the cemetery, noting the layout of the graves, pathways, trees, and other landmarks. Use your measuring tape or GPS device to measure distances between graves or plot out the dimensions of the cemetery. This will become very useful if you plan to digitize your cemetery. 4. Document Details: Take notes or photographs of any important details, such as the names and dates on grave markers, the types of graves (e.g., headstones, mausoleums), and any unique features of the cemetery. 5. Create a Map: Once you've gathered all the necessary information, you can create a map of the cemetery. You can use mapping software, like EverArk, or apps like Google Earth, GIS (Geographic Information Systems) software, or even simple drawing tools to create your map. Include labels for graves, pathways, and landmarks to make the map easy to understand. 6. Review and Revise: After creating the initial map, review it for accuracy and completeness. Make any necessary revisions or additions to ensure that the map accurately represents the cemetery. 7. Share or Publish: Depending on your purpose for mapping the cemetery, you may want to share the map with others, such as genealogists, historians, or the local community. You can publish the map online using EverArk's cemetery management software, in a local history book, or in other formats to make it accessible to others who may be interested. And, of course, remember to be respectful when mapping a cemetery and consider the privacy and sensitivities of those who may have loved ones buried there. text: 06/27/2023 WHAT IS THE BEST WAY TO IMPLEMENT A CEMETERY SOFTWARE? Implementing cemetery software effectively requires careful planning and execution. Most software implementations fail, not because the software doesn't meet requirements, but because there's a lack of preparation and understanding of the implementation process. Here are some steps to consider for a successful cemetery software implementation: Define Cemetery Objectives and Requirements Clearly define your cemetery objectives and the specific requirements the software needs to fulfill. Identify key stakeholders and involve them in the planning process to ensure their needs and expectations are considered. Make sure the end-users are involved in all discussions and aspects of the implementation since the success of the implementation is a direct result of their buy-in and adoption of the cemetery system. Establish a Cemetery Project Team Create a dedicated project team with representatives from different departments or teams that will be impacted by the cemetery software implementation. Assign clear roles and responsibilities to team members and establish effective communication channels. Make sure there is at least one individual that will become the super user of the cemetery software. Develop an Implementation Plan Create a detailed plan that outlines the implementation timeline, tasks, milestones, and dependencies. Identify any necessary data migration or integration requirements. Set realistic deadlines and allocate resources accordingly. If you don't have dedicated resources to assign to the implementation, make sure to consider their current workload when setting a timeline and assigning tasks. Prepare the Infrastructure Ensure that the necessary hardware, network, and infrastructure are in place to support the software. Verify that the system requirements align with your existing IT environment and make any necessary upgrades or adjustments. In today's cloud-based infrastructures, this can be as simple as making sure your users can access the software from their portable devices, such as laptops and tablets. Data Migration and Cleansing If you are migrating data from existing systems to the new software, plan and execute the data migration process carefully. Cleanse and validate the data to ensure accuracy and integrity. This is generally the biggest bottleneck and time-consuming exercise of any implementation, but also the most important. Like anything, garbage in is garbage out and that holds true for all cemetery software implementations. Customization and Configuration If the cemetery software allows for customization or configuration, work closely with the cemetery software vendor or internal IT team to tailor the software to your specific requirements. Balance customization with the need to maintain the software's core functionality and support future upgrades. Simple configurations like adding your cemetery logo, updating the color scheme, and customizing the URL will go a long way for improving the user experience. Cemetery Training and Education Provide comprehensive training to users who will be utilizing the cemetery software. Offer both general training on the software's features and functions, as well as specific training based on individual roles and responsibilities. Consider offering training materials, user guides, and ongoing support to facilitate the learning process. A good cemetery software will have all of this built into the software so you can learn at your own pace, especially if the training materials is supported by online training videos. Test and Validate Conduct thorough testing of the cemetery software to identify and resolve any issues or bugs. Develop test scenarios and use cases that cover various functionalities and business processes. Involve end-users in the testing process to gather feedback and ensure the software meets their needs. It is critical for the long-term success of the cemetery software that the end-users are comfortable with the cemetery software before is goes live. Cemetery Rollout and User Adoption Plan a phased rollout of the cemetery software to minimize disruption and allow for gradual adoption. Communicate the benefits of the software to users, address any concerns, and provide ongoing support during the transition period. Monitor user adoption and address any issues that arise. Evaluate and Optimize Continuously evaluate the cemetery software's performance, user feedback, and alignment with your objectives. Collect data and metrics to assess the impact of the cemetery software on your business processes and outcomes. Use this information to optimize and improve the software implementation as needed. Remember that successful cemetery software implementation requires collaboration, effective communication, and the involvement of key stakeholders and end-users throughout the process. It's important to be adaptable and responsive to feedback and make necessary adjustments along the way. title: Key Cemetery Management Challenges | Cemetery Software - EVERARK
description: What are some of the key challenges cemetery managers and administrators face in today's world.
text: 02/28/2023 WHAT ARE KEY CHALLENGES CEMETERY MANAGERS FACE? Cemetery management is an important responsibility for any community, as it involves preserving the final resting place of loved ones and ensuring that the cemetery remains a peaceful and respectful space for mourners. However, cemetery management can also be a challenging task, as there are many different factors that can impact the maintenance and upkeep of a cemetery. In this blog post, we will explore some of the key challenges faced by cemetery managers and administrators. Aging Infrastructure for Cemeteries Many cemeteries have been around for decades or even centuries, which means that their infrastructure and facilities may be outdated or in need of repair. This can include everything from deteriorating headstones and monuments to aging plumbing and drainage systems. Cemetery managers must balance the need for historic preservation with the need for modernization, ensuring that the cemetery remains functional and accessible while also preserving its historical significance. Cemeteries Have Limited Land and Space As urban areas grow and land becomes scarcer, many cemeteries are facing the challenge of limited space. This can make it difficult to accommodate new burials and can result in overcrowding, which can compromise the dignity and sanctity of the cemetery. Cemetery managers must be proactive in finding solutions to this challenge, which may include expanding the cemetery or exploring alternative burial options such as cremation. Environmental Factors for Cemeteries are Becoming More Important Cemeteries are subject to a wide range of environmental factors that can impact their maintenance and upkeep. For example, extreme weather events such as heavy rain or snow can cause erosion and damage to headstones and monuments, while drought or extreme heat can lead to dry and cracked soil. Cemetery managers must be prepared to respond to these environmental challenges, which may involve implementing new landscaping techniques, drainage systems, or other solutions. Cemeteries Face Financial Constraints Like any organization, cemeteries must operate within a budget, which can sometimes limit their ability to address key management challenges. This may include a lack of funding for repairs or improvements, or limited staff resources to manage day-to-day operations. Cemetery managers must balance the need for financial stability with the need to provide quality services and care for the cemetery. Societal Attitudes Are Slow to Change Finally, cemetery management is also impacted by changing societal attitudes towards death and burial. In recent years, there has been a growing trend towards alternative burial options such as cremation, which can impact the demand for traditional burial plots. Cemetery managers must be aware of these trends and adapt their services and facilities to meet the evolving needs of their community. In conclusion, cemetery management is a complex and challenging task that requires careful attention to a wide range of factors. From aging infrastructure and limited space to environmental factors and changing societal attitudes, cemetery managers must be prepared to navigate a constantly evolving landscape in order to preserve the dignity and sanctity of the cemetery. By working proactively to address these challenges, cemetery managers can ensure that their cemetery remains a peaceful and respectful space for generations to come. One challenge no cemetery should have to face is poor technology. text: 06/03/2025 UNLOCKING THE PAST: A Step-by-Step Guide to Mapping a Cemetery Have you ever wandered through a cemetery, captivated by the stories that lay beneath the surface? Mapping a cemetery not only honors those who rest there but also uncovers rich histories waiting to be told. This step-by-step guide will equip you with essential techniques and insights to create a comprehensive map, transforming your experience from a simple stroll to an enlightening journey into the past. From choosing the right tools to documenting grave markers and inscriptions, you ll learn how to navigate the often-overlooked details that bring these resting places to life. Whether you re a genealogist seeking family roots or a history enthusiast curious about your local community, this guide will empower you to unlock the secrets of the cemetery while preserving its legacy for future generations. Let s embark on this fascinating exploration together, and discover how mapping a cemetery can reveal the stories that time has hidden away. Importance of Cemetery Mapping Wandering through a cemetery is like stepping back in time, where each gravestone tells a story of a life once lived. Cemetery mapping serves a crucial role in preserving these stories, ensuring that they are not lost to the ravages of time. By creating a detailed map of a cemetery, you are essentially piecing together a historical narrative that provides invaluable insights into the past. This practice is especially significant for genealogists who are tracing family roots, historians uncovering local heritage, and community members who wish to honor their ancestors. Cemetery mapping is more than just a hobby; it is a valuable contribution to historical preservation. Often, cemeteries are subject to neglect, vandalism, or natural decay, which can lead to the loss of important historical data. Detailed maps and records help safeguard this information, allowing future generations to access and learn from it. Moreover, accurate cemetery maps can assist in various research projects, from demographic studies to the examination of cultural and social trends over time. The importance of cemetery mapping extends beyond individual interests. It fosters a sense of community by bringing people together with a shared goal of preserving and understanding their collective history. When communities engage in cemetery mapping projects, they not only honor those who have passed but also strengthen their connection to the past and each other. This collaborative effort can also raise awareness about the need for cemetery conservation, prompting local authorities and organizations to take action in preserving these historical sites. Tools and Equipment Needed for Mapping Embarking on a cemetery mapping project requires a combination of traditional tools and modern technology. The first essential tool is a high-quality GPS device, which will allow you to accurately record the coordinates of each grave. This precision is crucial for creating an accurate and detailed map. Additionally, a measuring tape or laser distance measurer will help you take precise measurements of the distances between graves and other landmarks within the cemetery. Another indispensable tool is a digital camera or a smartphone with a good camera. Photographs of each grave marker, inscription, and unique feature will serve as visual documentation that can be referenced later. Notebooks and pens are also necessary for jotting down observations, sketching layouts, and recording any additional information that may not be captured with a camera or GPS device. It s important to have a sturdy clipboard or field notebook to keep your notes organized and protected from the elements. In addition to these basic tools, consider using mapping software or applications designed specifically for cemetery documentation. Programs like ArcGIS, Google Earth, and specialized cemetery mapping apps can help you create detailed and interactive maps. These tools often come with features that allow you to layer different types of data, such as historical records, photographs, and GPS coordinates, providing a comprehensive view of the cemetery. Investing in these tools and equipment will streamline the mapping process and enhance the accuracy and detail of your final map. Understanding Cemetery Records and Documentation Before you start mapping a cemetery, it's essential to familiarize yourself with the existing records and documentation. These records often include burial registers, plot maps, and historical documents that provide valuable information about the individuals buried in the cemetery. By reviewing these documents, you can gain insights into the cemetery's layout, the historical context of the burials, and any notable individuals or events associated with the site. Burial registers are a key resource, as they typically contain the names of the deceased, dates of death, and plot locations. These registers can help you cross-reference the information you gather during your mapping project, ensuring accuracy and completeness. Plot maps, on the other hand, provide a visual representation of the cemetery's layout, showing the arrangement of graves and any significant landmarks. Historical documents, such as obituaries, family histories, and local archives, can offer additional context and enrich the stories behind the graves you document. It's also beneficial to reach out to local historical societies, genealogical groups, and cemetery associations. These organizations often have extensive knowledge and resources that can aid in your research. They may also be able to provide access to records that are not publicly available or offer guidance on best practices for cemetery mapping. Building relationships with these groups can enhance your project and create opportunities for collaboration. Understanding and utilizing cemetery records and documentation is a crucial step in the mapping process. It not only helps ensure the accuracy of your map but also enriches the historical narrative you are creating. By integrating this information into your project, you can provide a more comprehensive and meaningful representation of the cemetery and its significance. Step-by-Step Process for Mapping a Cemetery Mapping a cemetery is a meticulous process that requires careful planning and execution. The first step is to conduct a preliminary survey of the site. This involves walking through the cemetery to get a sense of its layout, noting any areas that may require special attention, such as sections with older or damaged graves. During this survey, take preliminary photographs and make rough sketches to help you plan your mapping strategy. Next, create a detailed plan for your mapping project. This plan should outline the specific areas you will map, the tools and equipment you will use, and the methodology you will follow. It's important to establish a systematic approach to ensure that no graves are overlooked and that your data collection is consistent. Consider dividing the cemetery into manageable sections and mapping one section at a time. Once your plan is in place, you can begin the actual mapping process. Start by using your GPS device to record the coordinates of each grave. Take measurements of the distances between graves and other landmarks to create an accurate layout. Document each grave marker by taking photographs and noting any inscriptions or unique features. Be sure to record all this information in your notebook or digital device for later reference. After you have collected all the necessary data, the next step is to compile and organize it. Use your mapping software or application to input the GPS coordinates, measurements, and photographs. This will allow you to create a detailed and interactive map of the cemetery. Review your data to ensure accuracy and completeness, making any necessary adjustments. The final step is to create a detailed map and report that includes all the information you have gathered. This report should provide a comprehensive overview of the cemetery, including the layout, the location of each grave, and any historical or contextual information. By following this step-by-step process, you can create an accurate and meaningful map that preserves the history and significance of the cemetery. Techniques for Accurate Measurements and Data Collection Accurate measurements and data collection are the foundation of a successful cemetery mapping project. One effective technique for ensuring precision is to use a grid system. By dividing the cemetery into a grid, you can systematically map each section and ensure that no graves are missed. Use stakes and string to mark out the grid, and take measurements from fixed points within each section. This method provides a clear and organized framework for your mapping efforts. When taking measurements, it's important to use reliable tools, such as a measuring tape or a laser distance measurer. These tools can help you obtain precise distances between graves and other landmarks. Always double-check your measurements to ensure accuracy, and record them in your field notebook or digital device. Consistency is key, so use the same measurement technique throughout the entire mapping process. In addition to measurements, accurate data collection requires detailed documentation of each grave marker. Take clear and high-resolution photographs of each marker, capturing the inscriptions and any unique features. Use a notebook or digital device to record the names, dates, and any other information inscribed on the markers. It's also helpful to make sketches of the grave markers and their surroundings to provide additional context. Another important aspect of data collection is to record the GPS coordinates of each grave. Use a high-quality GPS device to obtain precise coordinates, and cross-reference them with your measurements and photographs. This will help you create an accurate and detailed map of the cemetery. By employing these techniques, you can ensure that your data collection is thorough and precise, resulting in a comprehensive and accurate cemetery map. Creating a Cemetery Map: Software and Applications In the digital age, creating a cemetery map has been greatly simplified by the availability of specialized software and applications. These tools offer a range of features that enhance the accuracy and detail of your map, making it easier to document and visualize the cemetery. One popular option is ArcGIS, a powerful geographic information system (GIS) software that allows you to create detailed maps with multiple layers of data. With ArcGIS, you can input GPS coordinates, measurements, and photographs to create a comprehensive and interactive map. The downside is that ArcGIS can be expensive and difficult to learn. Google Earth is another valuable tool for cemetery mapping. This application allows you to overlay your data onto satellite imagery, providing a detailed and accurate visual representation of the cemetery. You can input GPS coordinates, add markers, and create custom layers to highlight specific areas or features. Google Earth also offers tools for measuring distances and areas, which can enhance the accuracy of your map. This solution is free and integrates automatically with EverArk, a leading cemetery management software with online interactive mapping. These applications often come with features tailored to cemetery documentation, such as templates for recording grave marker information, tools for creating plot maps, and options for generating reports. Some popular cemetery mapping apps include EverArk and Find A Grave. These tools can streamline the mapping process and provide a user-friendly interface for managing your data. description: ​Whether we want to think about it or not, we are all destined to attend our own funeral, so it is smart to make plans for it now. Here's what to avoid.
text: 5/24/2022 Mistakes to Avoid When Planning a Funeral Whether we want to think about it or not, we are all destined to attend our own funeral, so it is smart to make plans for it now. After all, it is your sendoff party and details matter, which is why you need to make the arrangements in advance to be sure your final wishes are honored. Planning your funeral means deciding the major and minor details of the event, so your friends and loved ones can feel your spirit as they are honoring your memory. When you fail to plan for your funeral or memorial service, the responsibility falls on the shoulders of a loved one who may not know all your likes and dislikes. This means that your casket may be surrounded by yellow roses when you hate yellow roses! Be mindful that planning someone else s funeral is not the most comfortable position to be in, and the person responsible may make decisions under pressure that you disagree with if you could. To avoid the pitfalls of having someone else plan your funeral, it is best to handle this yourself. However, just because you are taking the reins by ironing out all the details, mistakes can still happen. Dodge Common Mistakes When Planning Your Funeral Even if you do not have one foot in the grave, planning your funeral now is a step in the right direction. Nevertheless, it is important to tackle the planning process in a constructive manner and educate yourself to avoid making mistakes, so your funeral or memorial service is everything you hope it will be. Keep your sense of humor. Death is a part of life, so do not take yourself and the process of arranging your funeral too seriously. Warm up for the big decisions by beginning with the finer details. Consider the kinds of flowers you want featured, or maybe you do not want any flowers at all. Think about the music you want playing. Do you have a favorite CD or MP3 song mix? Maybe you would prefer to have your sendoff accompanied by a pianist or violinist. Do not be afraid to spice things up. Remember, it is your final good-bye. If you want your funeral to be a happy event by turning it into a dance party, arrange for a DJ and a bartender! Your funeral can be as solemn or boisterous as you like. Appoint trusted people to manage your plans. This is the most important part of the planning process. Once you have decided on all the details of your funeral, choose three people you believe will honor your wishes. Failing to reserve at least three people is a huge mistake because one or more of them may unfortunately pass on before you. Be sure to ask them if they want the responsibility of making sure your funeral arrangements go off without a hitch. Should they politely refuse, thank them and approach other family members and friends. If you do not have anyone to handle your plans, reach out to a priest or an attorney. Choose a location. This decision is largely based on how you plan to be buried, or not. If you want to be laid to rest in a cemetery, plan for a traditional funeral service and decide if you want it to happen in a church or similar location. If you prefer to be cremated or desire a green burial, arrange a memorial service to happen at a place that is capable of catering to large gatherings. If you want alcohol at your service, make sure the establishment can legally serve beer and wine. If you want to have your funeral or memorial service outdoors in a cemetery, a garden, or at the beach, keep in mind that you may die during a month with very hot or very cold weather. To avoid giving your guests an unpleasant experience, arrange a backup plan in case inclement weather ruins your original plans. Gather as much information as possible. What you don t know can impact your funeral plans and create setbacks in your life. For example, if you fail to research the funeral homes in your area, you may end up making reservations with a subpar funeral parlor that goes out of business. Hopefully, your money is quickly reimbursed, but this is not always the case. Most people facing the end of their life do not have the time, energy, and resources available to wait for refunds because they are busy crossing things off their bucket list. There are no stupid questions! Planning your own funeral will cause many questions to crop up in your mind, and voicing these concerns is vital. Not getting the answers you need to make informed decisions is a recipe for disaster. Furthermore, if you feel unclear about something or believe there has been a miscommunication, never be afraid to ask for written clarification. Failing to do this may lead to you being planted beside the wrong tree in the green burial garden. Research as much as you can about funerary details and leave no stone unturned. This is especially true when it comes to the different kinds of burials available, or you may decide to be cremated. Regardless of what you decide, it is important to choose the option that gives you the most comfort. While books are valuable tools, it is helpful to gather answers and opinions from multiple sources before making any final decisions. Never allow price to become a deciding factor. While most of us have a set budget and not a whole lot of wiggle room, if a service or item such as an urn seems overpriced, do not allow yourself to be talked into anything until you have shopped around. After all, the last thing you need is buyer s remorse. On the opposite extreme, if a price seems too good to be true, it probably is. Planning Your Funeral in Advance is a Smart Decision While planning your own funeral is not an easy thing to do, once this task is complete, people report experiencing peace of mind and a quiet reassurance that their wishes will be honored. They also feel satisfied that they have done all they can to alleviate future stress from their loved ones. In addition to removing a great weight from your shoulders and that of your family members, people who plan their own funerals report saving money on products and services that will become more expensive as time goes on. If you need assistance planning your funeral, reach out to the resources within your community that can provide guidance such as funeral directors, counselors, and clergy members. Nevertheless, if you are more comfortable completing the process in the privacy of your home, EverArk software has helped many people accomplish this and allows them to plan the details of their funeral without feeling rushed. EverArk also gives you the ability to create a digital legacy that your loved ones will cherish for a lifetime. You may even choose to display this during your funeral or memorial service, so all your guests can enjoy seeing you in a montage of photos and videos set to your favorite music. To learn how EverArk can take the stress out of planning your funeral, request a demo today! Previous Next

text: 2/19/2026 Cemetery Management Software Efficient Cemetery Plot Inventory Management: Tips & Best Practices Tips and best practices for cemetery plot management. Efficient cemetery plot inventory management is vital for maintaining order and providing peace of mind. Discover essential tips and best practices to streamline your processes. Understanding Cemetery Plot Inventory Management Cemetery plot inventory management is the systematic process of cataloging and organizing burial plots within a cemetery. This involves documenting details such as the location, availability, ownership, and status of each plot. Effective management ensures that the cemetery operates smoothly, providing families with the assurance that their loved ones' final resting places are well-maintained and easily accessible. Given the sensitive nature of the business, it is crucial to handle these records with accuracy and care to avoid any potential issues or misunderstandings. Managing cemetery plots is not just about keeping track of available spaces; it also involves historical records, ensuring that the legacy and heritage associated with the burial grounds are preserved. This includes maintaining detailed records of all interments, including dates, names, and any relevant inscriptions. This information can be invaluable for genealogical research, providing a rich source of data for historians and family members alike. Furthermore, cemetery plot inventory management is essential from a legal standpoint. Accurate records help to comply with local regulations and zoning laws, ensuring that the cemetery operates within the legal framework. Mismanagement can lead to legal disputes, financial penalties, and damage to the cemetery's reputation. Therefore, implementing a robust inventory management system is not only beneficial but necessary for the smooth operation of any cemetery. Importance of Efficient Inventory Management in Cemeteries Efficient inventory management in cemeteries is pivotal for several reasons. Firstly, it ensures that the cemetery can meet the needs of the community it serves. By keeping precise records of available plots, cemetery managers can provide accurate information to families making burial arrangements, which is particularly important during emotionally challenging times. This transparency helps build trust and confidence in the cemetery's operations. Secondly, efficient management aids in the financial health of the cemetery. By knowing exactly how many plots are available and where they are located, managers can optimize the use of space and plan for future expansions. This can lead to better financial planning and resource allocation, ensuring that the cemetery remains sustainable in the long term. Additionally, well-maintained records can facilitate quicker transactions and reduce administrative overhead, leading to cost savings. Lastly, efficient inventory management plays a critical role in the overall maintenance and aesthetic appeal of the cemetery. Properly managed plots ensure that the grounds are kept orderly and beautiful, reflecting respect and dignity for those interred there. This also helps in preventing issues such as overgrown plots, misplaced markers, or accidental disturbances during new burials. In essence, efficient inventory management contributes to the overall integrity and reputation of the cemetery. Common Challenges in Cemetery Plot Management Cemetery plot management comes with its own set of challenges, many of which stem from the historical nature of the records involved. One common issue is the transition from paper-based records to digital systems. Many cemeteries have decades, if not centuries, of records that need to be accurately digitized. This process can be time-consuming and prone to errors if not handled carefully. Ensuring that all historical data is correctly transferred and categorized requires meticulous attention to detail and often, specialized software. Another significant challenge is maintaining the accuracy of records over time. With multiple interments happening regularly, it's easy for records to become outdated or incorrect. Human errors in data entry, changes in plot ownership, and the physical alteration of the cemetery grounds can all contribute to discrepancies. Regular audits and updates are necessary to ensure the ongoing accuracy of the inventory, but these tasks can be labor-intensive and require dedicated resources. Space management is another critical issue. As cemeteries fill up, finding available plots that meet the needs of families can become increasingly difficult. This is particularly challenging in urban areas where space is at a premium. Effective inventory management must include strategies for maximizing space utilization, such as planning for future expansions or considering alternative interment options like columbariums for cremated remains. Balancing the need for new plots with the preservation of existing gravesites is a delicate act that requires careful planning and foresight. Best Practices for Cemetery Plot Inventory Tracking Implementing best practices for cemetery plot inventory tracking can significantly enhance the efficiency and accuracy of cemetery operations. One of the foremost practices is the adoption of a standardized system for recording plot information. This includes using a consistent format for documenting details such as plot location, ownership, interment dates, and any associated fees. Standardization ensures that all records are uniform, making it easier to retrieve and interpret data when needed. Another best practice is the regular auditing of records. Periodic reviews help identify and rectify discrepancies in the inventory, ensuring that the database remains up-to-date. Audits should include cross-referencing physical plot locations with digital records to verify accuracy. This practice not only maintains the integrity of the inventory but also helps in identifying any unauthorized changes or errors that may have occurred over time. Engaging with families and the community is also an essential aspect of effective inventory tracking. Keeping open lines of communication allows families to report any changes or issues with their plots, which can then be promptly updated in the records. Additionally, providing families with access to their records through an online portal can enhance transparency and trust. This practice not only improves customer satisfaction but also reduces the administrative burden on cemetery staff by enabling self-service options for plot information. Utilizing Technology for Inventory Management The integration of technology into cemetery plot inventory management has revolutionized the way cemeteries operate. One of the most impactful technological advancements is the use of Geographic Information Systems (GIS). GIS allows for the precise mapping of cemetery plots, providing a visual representation of the entire cemetery layout. This technology makes it easier to locate specific plots, plan for future expansions, and manage the overall space more effectively. GIS can also be integrated with other management systems to provide a comprehensive overview of the cemetery's operations. Another vital technological tool is cemetery management software. These specialized programs are designed to handle all aspects of cemetery operations, from plot sales and record-keeping to maintenance scheduling and financial management. By centralizing all information in one system, cemetery managers can streamline their processes and improve data accuracy. Features such as automated reminders for maintenance tasks, digital record storage, and online customer portals enhance operational efficiency and customer service. The use of mobile technology has also become increasingly prevalent in cemetery management. Mobile devices equipped with inventory management apps allow staff to update records in real-time while they are in the field. This immediate data entry reduces the risk of errors and ensures that the inventory is always current. Mobile technology also enables staff to quickly access information when assisting families, providing a higher level of service and support. Developing a Cemetery Plot Inventory System Developing a robust cemetery plot inventory system begins with a clear understanding of the cemetery's specific needs and challenges. The first step is to conduct a comprehensive assessment of the current inventory management practices. This includes evaluating existing records, identifying any gaps or inconsistencies, and determining the tools and resources currently in use. This assessment provides a baseline from which to develop a more effective system. Once the assessment is complete, the next step is to select the appropriate technology and software to support the inventory system. This may involve choosing a cemetery management software that offers the desired features, such as GIS integration, digital record-keeping, and customer portals. It's essential to select a solution that is scalable and can grow with the cemetery's needs. Additionally, the software should be user-friendly to ensure that all staff can effectively utilize it. After selecting the technology, the system needs to be implemented and tested. This involves migrating existing records into the new system, setting up user accounts, and configuring any necessary integrations. It's crucial to conduct thorough testing to ensure that all features are functioning correctly and that data has been accurately transferred. Training staff on the new system is also a vital component of the implementation process, as it ensures that everyone is proficient in using the new tools and can effectively manage the inventory. Regular Maintenance and Updates of Inventory Records Regular maintenance and updates of inventory records are critical to ensuring the accuracy and reliability of the cemetery plot inventory system. One of the key practices is conducting periodic audits of the records. These audits should involve cross-referencing digital records with physical plot locations to verify accuracy. Any discrepancies found during the audit should be promptly corrected to maintain the integrity of the inventory. Another important aspect of record maintenance is staying up-to-date with any changes or updates related to plot ownership, interments, or other relevant information. This includes promptly recording new burials, changes in ownership, and any alterations to the cemetery layout. Keeping records current ensures that the inventory remains accurate and reduces the risk of errors or misunderstandings. In addition to regular updates, it's also important to back up inventory records regularly. This protects against data loss due to technical issues, accidental deletions, or other unforeseen events. Implementing a robust backup strategy, including both on-site and off-site backups, ensures that records are secure and can be quickly restored if needed. This practice provides an additional layer of protection and peace of mind for both cemetery managers and families. Training Staff on Inventory Management Procedures Training staff on inventory management procedures is essential to ensure the smooth operation of the cemetery plot inventory system. Comprehensive training programs should be developed to cover all aspects of the inventory management process, including data entry, record maintenance, and the use of any relevant technology or software. Training should be tailored to the specific needs of each role within the cemetery, ensuring that all staff members are equipped with the knowledge and skills they need to perform their duties effectively. One effective training method is hands-on practice with the inventory management system. This allows staff to become familiar with the software and tools they will be using, and provides an opportunity to address any questions or concerns. Role-playing scenario

text: 10/04/2023 HOW DO YOU PREPARE FOR DEATH? In our first blog, What is a Celebration of Life ? , we discussed what it means and what a Digital Legacy is. In our second blog, we discuss preparing for one's eventual passing. It involves a range of practical and emotional considerations. Here's a general outline of steps someone might take: Legal Documents: Create or update important legal documents, including a will, living will (advance healthcare directive), and power of attorney. These documents outline your wishes for medical care, financial matters, and the distribution of your assets. A good digital legacy app will help you organize your end-of-life documents. Estate Planning: Consider consulting with a lawyer to ensure that your estate is organized and your assets are properly managed and distributed according to your wishes. Digital Legacy: Decide how you want your digital presence and online accounts to be handled after your passing. This includes social media accounts, emails, and other digital assets. EverArk's celebration of life app has a Digital Vault to help you manage your digital presence and online accounts after one's passing. Healthcare Wishes: Communicate your healthcare preferences to your loved ones and establish a healthcare proxy or durable power of attorney for healthcare decisions. Funeral and Burial Arrangements: Outline your preferences for your funeral, burial, or memorial service. This can ease the burden on your loved ones during a difficult time. If you are using a digital legacy app, you can prepare your notices and arrangements in advance. Financial Matters: Make sure your loved ones are aware of your financial accounts, assets, and any debts. Consider establishing a trust or naming beneficiaries where applicable. Personal Belongings: Think about what you want to happen to your personal belongings, heirlooms, and sentimental items. Communicate these wishes to your family. Organ Donation: If you wish to donate organs or tissues, make your intentions known and consider registering as an organ donor. Communication: Have open conversations with your loved ones about your wishes, financial matters, and end-of-life preferences. This can help avoid confusion and conflicts later. Emotional Support: Seek emotional support from friends, family, or a counselor. Preparing for death can be emotionally challenging, and having a support system can make a significant difference. Legacy Planning: Reflect on the legacy you want to leave behind. This could involve sharing life lessons, values, and memories with your loved ones. Review and Update: Regularly review and update your plans as circumstances change, such as major life events, legal changes, or shifts in your preferences. Remember, every individual's situation is unique. It's important to tailor your preparations to your own circumstances and consult with legal and financial professionals when needed. title: Plan for End of Life | Cemetery Software - EVERARK
description: Learn what you need to consider and know when pre-need planning for your or a loved one’s death. Here’s what you should do now to plan for the end of life.
text: 5/10/2022 Things You Should Do Now to Plan for End of Life Death may be an unpleasant idea for some people but planning for the end of your life not only makes your loved ones aware of your wishes, but also takes a significant weight from their shoulders during what will be a very difficult time. The beginning of the new year is the perfect time to create an end-of-life plan or re-evaluate your current one. Give Yourself and Your Family Peace of Mind Death is difficult to think about and even harder to discuss with those we love. However, it is necessary to take the time to make personal arrangements. It s a good idea to take the following actions while you are still healthy and of sound mind. Prepare your end-of-life planning documents. This is also known as Estate Planning because you are documenting your wishes regarding medical care and how your money, property, and valuables will be distributed upon your death. End-of-life planning documents include: Living Trust Allows you to manage your estate and assets while you are living. Living Will Ensures your wishes about medical decisions will be followed in the event you become incapacitated and unable to express them on your own. Last Will and Testament Legal document that details how your assets should be handled and who is responsible for your dependents when you pass away. Power of Attorney (POA) Provisions These are legal documents that must be drawn up by an attorney, and include Healthcare POA, Durable Medical POA, Healthcare Proxy, and Durable POA for Finances. By completing these forms, you are appointing someone to make legal, financial, medical, or business decisions on your behalf if you die or become incapacitated. Organ/Tissue Donor Designation These forms specify that you want your organs and tissue donated upon your death. Domestic Partnership Agreement This form is used to declare legal rights and responsibilities for long-term partnership. Decide between a Will and a Trust. A Trust protects you, your loved ones, and your legacy once you are gone. Trusts are not just for the wealthy. Anyone who owns property or assets valued at or above $160k should consider a Trust to avoid the painful and lengthy probate process. A Will is your written declaration about who should receive your assets upon your death. It also states who you have chosen to take responsibility for your minor children. If you are not ready to set up a Trust, a Will is a good place to start. Wills and Trusts can be modified at any time and should be reviewed annually. List your assets. Assets are the possessions you want passed down to your heirs. These items can include savings and checking accounts, cash, CDs, treasury bills, real estate and land, investments, stocks and bonds, pensions and retirement plans, life insurance policies, art and collectables, jewelry, and corporate assets if you own a business. Determine end-of-life housing. Let your loved ones know where you prefer to live out your days in the event you are unable to fully care for yourself. In-home care is a choice you can consider, but if you would rather enter an assisted living facility or a nursing home, do your research to discover which ones have the best reputation as well as their layout and amenities. Once you have narrowed down your choices, document your decision in writing and make your family aware of the specific locations you have chosen for end-of-life housing. Decide on funeral and burial arrangements . Determining this in advance is one of the kindest gifts you can give to your loved ones. When you die, they will be grieving, so making them aware of your final wishes beforehand will help the process be less painful and confusing for them. Choices of funerals include: Traditional Service A full funeral service that often happens in a church or funeral home. Viewing and Visitation Involves an open casket when possible, so friends and family can say their good-byes during a prearranged timeframe. Wake A gathering that happens in a home prior to a more formal service. Memorial Service A gathering that happens after a burial or cremation. Celebration of Life A type of memorial service that honors the deceased by celebrating their life. Committal or Graveside Service A brief gathering that occurs after a funeral and involves prayers and flowers. Scattering of Ashes A formal or informal ceremony that takes place after a loved one has been cremated. Choices of burials include: In-ground A loved one is laid to rest in a cemetery. Public or Private Mausoleum One s body (or ashes) is placed within an above-ground structure that houses several bodies or cremated remains. Lawn Crypt An above-ground structure that houses only one or two bodies or cremated remains. Cremation The process of disposing of a body by reducing it to ashes through combustion. Burial at Sea Involves releasing a body or ashes into the ocean from a boat. Green or Natural Burial Method that is gaining in popularity because it allows the body to naturally recycle into the earth through decomposition. Create your obituary, eulogy, and death notice. There is nothing wrong with a person writing their own obituary, eulogy, and death notice because doing so provides the opportunity to speak from the heart while it is still beating. After all, telling people you love them from beyond the grave will help comfort the grief-stricken and encourage closure for those experiencing feelings of guilt for past transgressions. Adding a touch of humor to your personal tributes will lighten the mood and inspire everyone to remember happier times, which will ease their pain. Remember to consider who will read your words aloud during the funeral or memorial service. Will it be a priest, attorney, or a sibling? If you have chosen a friend or relative, ask if they are comfortable with this responsibility before officially designating them for this role. Create a Digital Legacy Ever since the advent of social media, digital legacies have been gaining in popularity. This comes as no surprise because internet platforms have become depositories for the photos and videos of our most memorable experiences. Having photographic collections online makes it easy to transfer them to software platforms such as EverArk , so cherished memories can be viewed for generations to come. People also enjoy adding their favorite music and art to digital legacies. A digital legacy can even be created for a loved one who has already passed. Just find and upload your favorite photos and videos of them and add background music. Once you believe their digital legacy is complete, simply email the link to all the people who will enjoy viewing this special online memorial. Preparing for Death Brings Quietude Once you have your affairs in order, you will feel calm knowing that your final wishes will be honored. You will also experience peace of mind since you have articulated your thoughts and feelings. Now, you are free to enjoy the new year ahead and all the wonders life has to offer, including the promise of a peaceful rest. title: Trends in Green Burial | Cemetery Software - EVERARK
description: Learn more on what green interment trends are and how they are starting to take over traditional burial.
text: 7/7/2022 Trends in Green Burial As awareness grows about sustainable practices many people are adopting greener lifestyles. In more and more cases, they are choosing to forgo a traditional burial because it is very taxing to the earth and its resources. Green burials are eco-friendly ways to minimize your carbon footprint one last time. While most natural burials involve placing unembalmed bodies into the ground where they can merge with the earth, there are in fact several types of green burial methods available. It is important to become knowledgeable about the various kinds of green burials, so you can decide which one is best for you. Revolutionary Eco-Friendly Burial Techniques Mushroom Fiber Coffins Mycelium, which is a fungus-like bacterial colony, is being used to create innovative coffins that have been called Living Cocoons. Bob Hendrikx and his team at Loop created these biodegradable caskets as the ultimate way to help people return to nature. The magic happens at Loop lab at the Technical University of Delft. The team can grow one coffin within a week s time after mixing mycelium mushroom spores with wood chips using a coffin mold. Once the mycelium has grown through the wood chips, the casket is dried and ready to recycle a body weighing as much as 440 pounds. Mycelium is the green choice for casket construction because mushrooms are nature s greatest recyclers, according to Hendrikx. Fungi devour toxins and pollutants such as metals, oils and microplastics, then turns them into nutrients that enrich the soil and feed the surrounding plants. Once the mushroom coffin is buried, rainwater and ground water dissolve the coffin within 30 to 45 days. Thanks to the fungi, the body it surrounds decomposes in as little as 3 to 6 months rather than the decade or two it takes when encased within a traditional coffin. The price of a mushroom fiber coffin is about $2,400, which makes it much more financially feasible than a traditional casket. The Living Cocoon made its debut in The Netherlands in 2020. Hydro-cremation More people are choosing cremation over traditional burials. However, reducing a body to ash using extreme heat is not a very green method because the process is equivalent to driving five hundred miles in a gasoline powered vehicle. Developed in the early 1990s, alkaline hydrolysis, or hydro-cremation, is much more eco-friendly because the process involves the use of 95% water and 5% alkali to dissolve soft tissue, so only bones remain. The process takes approximately two to three hours. The bones are then dried and crushed into a powdery substance that is placed into an urn and returned to the family who can choose to bury or spread the ashes, or even have them turned into keepsakes such as gemstones. Hydro-cremation is ground-breaking because it is less impactful to the environment and uses considerably less energy than traditional cremation. However, there are moral arguments against the process because some people believe that it is not a dignified way to dispose of a body because the liquified remains are sent down the drain. Everyone considering hydro-cremation should conduct their own research before deciding if this method is right for them. Biodegradable Funeral Urns These eco-friendly vessels are designed to hold cremated ashes and dissolve once they are buried in the ground or placed into a body of water. They can be made of a variety of materials including ecological paper, recycled paper products, cloth, salt, cornstarch, clay, tree bark, palm leaves, and even olive pits. Biodegradable urns come in a wide variety of shapes, colors, and themes. While everyone is sure to find one that appeals to them, industry professionals recommend choosing an urn that is approved by the Green Burial Council . The Living Urn is a popular choice for those who want to minimize their carbon footprint after they depart. It is a bio urn and planting system that can grow a tree, plant, or flowers that are nourished by the cremated remains. The urn can eventually be placed into the ground, so it can biodegrade while the plant it holds lives on. Human Composting Scientifically known as Natural Organic Reduction (NOR), the process involves placing the decedent inside a steel container with wood chips, alfalfa, and straw. Heat and oxygen are applied to the vessel to increase the rate of decomposition by encouraging microbial growth. The contents of the container are blended throughout the decomposition process to break up the bones and ensure the body is fully composted. Once the process is complete, one cubic yard of soil remains, and medical implants are removed. The nutrient rich soil is returned to the family who will use it to create a flower garden or tree memorial dedicated to the deceased loved one. The human composting process takes four to six weeks and costs between $4,000 and $5,500. Transporting the body to the composting facility and delivering the soil to the family are often an extra cost. Natural Organic Reduction is eco-friendly because it uses 1/8 of the energy required for traditional cremation and saves one metric ton of carbon dioxide from entering the atmosphere. If NOR is something you want to consider, check with your state because it is not yet available everywhere. Tree Pod Burial Organic burial pods are expected to become a popular solution to the problems plaguing traditional burials. This unique concept was created by Italian designers Francesco D Angelo and Adriano Del Ferro. When they unveiled their conceptual tree pod burial system in 2016, they called it Capsula Mundi. According to the designers, the unembalmed body is wrapped in natural fiber cloth, then placed into an eco-friendly, egg-shaped pod. Once the pod is buried in the ground, a tree is planted directly on top. As the body decays, it feeds the tree with nutrients and microbes. Contribute to Science As more people become earth conscience, there are those who are choosing to donate their body to science. Deciding to forgo a burial altogether is a green choice in and of itself; however, allowing your remains to educate others makes an even greater impact. There are several avenues available should you decide to go this route. Medical schools are always in need of cadavers, but few people are aware that anthropologists and forensic scientists require them as well. Outdoor human decomposition research laboratories, or body farms , expose cadavers to nature s elements and adverse situations to discover how a body decomposes under specific circumstances. Their research is used to solve crimes by understanding how moisture, temperature, insects, and other variables uniquely affect a human body s decomposition. The researchers at body farms also use cadavers to learn how to determine the age, sex, and ancestry of a decedent by analyzing the measurements and characteristics of skulls and other bones. These facilities do more than educate scientists. They are also used to train cadaver dogs! If donating your remains to a body farm sounds like something you might want to consider, check out this article to learn more. Green Burials are More Than Just a Trend It is clear as a mountain stream that traditional burials are simply not feasible if we want a brighter future. When you live your life in ways that keep the planet healthy, it only makes sense to choose an eco-friendly burial or use your death to further scientific discovery. Deciding not to get embalmed is the first step, then you can opt for any of the eco-friendly methods discussed above. No matter what you decide, it is imperative that you notify a trusted relative or friend of your plans, so you can be sure that your final wishes will be honored. A software program called EverArk can help because it allows you to create a living trust. Using this state-of-the-art software safeguards your plans and allows you to make changes at any time. EverArk also provides you with the opportunity to design a digital legacy that your loved ones and future generations will cherish for life. title: Benefits of a Green Burial? | Cemetery Software - EVERARK
description: What is green burial, and what are its benefits? Learn about the history of green burial and why you should consider it over conventional burials.
text: 6/28/2022 What are the Benefits of a Green Burial? Green burials were originally known as natural burials because no formaldehyde-based embalming fluids were infused into the body prior to it being interred. Today, green burials are making a comeback for several reasons. However, it is important to know why natural burials were abandoned in the first place before you can understand why they are of great importance today. Misconceptions About Disease Killed the Natural Burial In the 1700s, a Scottish surgeon by the name of William Hunter invented the process of embalming and his brother John helped him provide this service to the public. Embalming was, in fact, greatly needed during this time because long distance travel had become increasingly popular, and people were dying far from home. Embalming slows down the body s decomposition, so the decedent could arrive home in good condition. During the turn of the 19th century, embalming was becoming a popular means of preparing dead bodies for viewing and burial. This practice became even more widespread once the Civil War was underway. During this era, sanitation reforms were being promoted throughout society as a war on filth was reaching critical mass. Of course, people who lived during this time were no strangers to death. Not only were communities losing countless men to the atrocities of war, but an inordinate number of deaths were occurring because of diseases such as measles, yellow fever, and cholera. Unfortunately, doctors were not yet aware of microorganisms such as bacteria and viruses, so they blamed the disease outbreaks on bad smells. As a result, they concluded that people were getting sick and dying from the foul odors emitted from trash and decaying corpses. Doctors and scientists believed they could cure diseases if they curbed the stench overwhelming their towns and cities. While their plan helped reduce the amount of trash in the streets, it put the brakes on natural burials. There were also laws enacted that made it illegal to bury an unembalmed body. On May 24th, 1861, embalming achieved a historical milestone. Dr. Thomas Holmes had been experimenting with modern embalming techniques, so when Colonel Elmer Ephraim Ellsworth was killed while removing a Confederate flag from a Virginia hotel, Dr. Holmes saw an opportunity. He wasted no time approaching President Lincoln about embalming Colonel Ellsworth s body and offered his services at no cost. Lincoln accepted his offer and soldiers were able to pay their respects to the Colonel as he lied in state at New York City Hall. Preserving the Dearly Departed Harms the Living The embalming process involves the injection of arterial fluids that help preserve dead bodies by slowing decomposition, which in turn eliminates the odors associated with decay. While this is beneficial in many ways, it results in just as many problems. The chemicals that are combined to make embalming fluid include preservatives, sanitizing agents, disinfectants, solvents, conditioners, and water. The main preservative is formaldehyde, which is held in the solution by methanol. The most common disinfectant used in the mixture is glutaraldehyde. Conditioners decrease acidity, deactivate certain drugs, and increase the absorption of the embalming fluid, which also includes dyes. These dyes work to improve the body s color and help the embalmer see the proper distribution of the embalming fluid. Humectants, or wetting agents, cause the body to appear hydrated, while anti-edemics reduce excessive fluids in the body. Funeral directors and morticians must be very careful when working with embalming fluid because it is extremely poisonous. Formaldehyde is a known carcinogen and is also classified as an allergen. Even a miniscule amount of formaldehyde can induce convulsions, stomach pains, diarrhea, vomiting, vertigo, and several other severe symptoms. Methanol is also highly toxic in very small doses. If an embalmer accidently exposes him or herself to embalming fluid, they can experience respiratory failure and even fall into a coma. Embalmed bodies cannot be placed directly into the ground because the toxic chemicals will leach into the environment. However, the caskets that hold the bodies also pose environmental problems. Modern caskets are not eco-friendly because they are resource-heavy due to the metal and precious woods that are used in their designs. Green Burials are Flourishing and for Good Reason! The 21st century is seeing a return to natural burials. People are becoming more health conscious and making choices that are safer for the environment. Thanks to scientific breakthroughs in the death industry, funeral directors and morticians can now work with embalming fluid that is nontoxic. While green burials do not require bodies to be embalmed, this process helps preserve the body long enough for loved ones to pay their respects at a viewing. Green embalming fluid is considered a safer alternative because it does not contain formaldehyde. Regardless, choosing to get embalmed is a very personal choice and some people choose to forgo this process. In addition to green burials being eco-friendly, there are several reasons to choose this process. Not only do these interments minimally impact the environment and conserve natural resources, but they also limit carbon emissions, protect the health of workers, and promote the restoration and preservation of dwindling habitats. When a body is returned to the earth, it feeds microbes in the soil and benefits other lifeforms, too. This is a big reason why it is important for bodies to be buried in their natural state, which can include biodegradable caskets, shrouds, and urns. Green burials are also very cost-effective and those who decide to go this route have peace of mind knowing they are giving the earth one last gift by reducing their carbon footprint. Choosing a Green Burial is a Wise Decision. People who decide on a green burial are making a healthy and responsible choice. However, one needs to know that there are three kinds of green cemeteries. This is the reason why it is important to research the ones in your community prior to choosing one. Hybrid cemeteries combine traditional burial sites with green sections that allow unembalmed bodies to be buried in biodegradable caskets or shrouds. Keep in mind that such cemeteries may still use harmful pesticides and non-native turf and plants. If you do not object to these landscaping practices, this may be the right choice for you. Natural burial grounds have strict rules and regulations. They do not have a traditional cemetery section and only cater to the burial of unembalmed bodies. They also do not allow cement and metal vaults, marble or stone grave markers, and caskets made of non-biodegradable materials. Natural burial grounds follow stringent guidelines that reduce waste and conserve energy as a means of improving sustainability. If you are looking for reassurance that your natural burial plot will remain in pristine condition forever, gain supreme peace of mind by choosing to be interred at a conservation burial site. Owned and maintained by independent conservation groups such as a land trust, this type of green burial ground promises to endure as a conservation land or easement that will always be preserved in its natural state. Conservation burial sites follow the same strict protocols as natural burial grounds. title: What is the Death Positive Movement | Cemetery Software - EVERARK
description: What is death positive movement, and how did it come about? Learn how EverArk is supporting this movement through its digital legacy software.
text: 5/18/2022 What is the Death Positive Movement? Those who practice Death Positive Movement hold the belief that death is not a morbid or taboo topic and should be discussed openly. People and groups who promote this viewpoint believe that the foundation of a healthy society must include honest conversations about death and dying. A Timeline: Breathing Life into the Death Positive Movement The birth of the Death Positive Movement happened in 1974 when the first hospice opened in the UK. The movement gained momentum in 1978 when the U.S. Department of Health, Education, and Welfare declared that the hospice movement as a concept for the care of the terminally ill and their families is a viable concept and one which holds out a means of providing more humane care for Americans dying of terminal illness while possibly reducing costs. As such, it is the proper subject of federal support. During the 1980s, palliative care was gaining popularity in the United States, which brought about the Death Acceptance Movement. People found that they appreciated how palliative care offers an interdisciplinary approach to caring for individuals living with illnesses that made everyday life difficult and restrictive. Furthermore, palliative care enhances a person s quality of life and improves the overall treatment of the terminally ill. It also works to help patients and their families cope with impending death. These advancements encouraged death acceptance advocates to argue that society should not be focused on unnecessary and costly medical interventions that usually prolong suffering. Over the years, they have been successfully promoting the belief that it was much more beneficial and productive to put energy toward enhanced care and improving quality of life. The 1990s saw the introduction of the Green Burial Movement, which has its roots in the natural burial process. Green burials are the closest to what nature intended for the disposal of a body because it involves placing a deceased person into the ground without the use of embalming fluids or a casket. Green burials are part of the Death Positive Movement because people experience great comfort knowing that this eco-friendly method will allow them to become one with the earth. In 2011, a man named Jon Underwood contributed to the Death Positive Movement by creating a social franchise called Death Caf s. People gather at these establishments to discuss death while enjoying cake and tea. Underwood s unique endeavor shines a light on this necessary part of life and provides an outlet for the grief-stricken. They also encourage people to make the most of their lives. Today, Death Caf s exist in 78 countries. When Covid-19 mandates prevented people from meeting in-person, Death Caf s entered cyberspace. Also in 2011, a young funeral director named Caitlin Doughty was left horrified after witnessing how the funeral industry was failing families financially and emotionally. To combat these deceitful practices, Doughty founded The Order of the Good Death and a web series titled Ask a Mortician , which answers death questions and promotes death positivity. The series has been viewed over 200 million times and continues to help people from all walks of life adopt a more optimistic view of death. The 8 Doctrines of the Death Positive Movement I believe that by hiding death and dying behind closed doors we do more harm than good to our society. I believe that the culture of silence around death should be broken through discussion, gatherings, art, innovation, and scholarship. I believe that talking about and engaging with my inevitable death is not morbid but displays a natural curiosity about the human condition. I believe that the dead body is not dangerous, and that everyone should be empowered (should they wish to be) to be involved in care for their own dead. I believe that the laws that govern death, dying, and end-of-life care should ensure that a person s wishes are honored, regardless of sexual, gender, racial, or religious identity. I believe that my death should be handled in a way that does not do great harm to the environment. I believe that my family and friends should know my end-of-life wishes, and that I should have the necessary paperwork to back-up those wishes. I believe that my open, honest advocacy around death can make a difference, and can change culture. Changing Minds and Attitudes About Death for a Better Life It is common knowledge that people are afraid of things that they do not understand. Death falls into this category because it is one of the great mysteries of life. There are too many unknowns. When you have a large portion of the population that fears this natural part of life, the result is a fearful society, which is not healthy. Since its inception in the 1970s, the Death Positive Movement has been working toward bettering society by changing people s perspective about death. Thanks to the brave trailblazers and supporters of this crusade, the dark stigma surrounding death is, unironically, dying. The more this movement spreads, the fear associated with death and dying will be replaced with wisdom and grace, so acceptance and healing can happen at a faster pace.
